The key issue is not only whether I believe I can act objectively but whether a reasonable person would have confidence in the independence of the valuation.
Valuation.referral: A conflict is when you know both parties.
referralWhy: Conflicts can arise in many ways including financial professional or prior involvement issues
challenge: What is an actual conflict versus a perceived conflict?
How would you check for conflicts?
Can all conflicts be managed?
When would you decline an instruction?
keyPoints: Valuers must act objectively
Conflicts can be actual potential or perceived
Conflicts should be checked before accepting instructions
Some conflicts cannot be managed and require declining the instruction

Valuation.q: What is valuation uncertainty?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because valuation is not always a precise exercise — candidates must recognise uncertainty, explain it clearly and avoid misleading the client.
Valuation.pass: Valuation uncertainty arises when there is less confidence in the valuation conclusion due to factors such as limited comparable evidence, market volatility, unusual property characteristics or lack of information. The valuer should explain the uncertainty and its potential impact to the client.
Valuation.high: Valuation uncertainty arises where the valuation conclusion is less certain because of market conditions, limited evidence, unusual asset characteristics, incomplete information or rapidly changing circumstances. It does not mean the valuation is wrong — it means the degree of confidence attached to the valuation is affected and the client should be made aware. I would record the uncertainty in the report clearly and proportionately, avoiding generic caveats. I would advise the client how the uncertainty affects reliance on the valuation and whether further evidence, sensitivity analysis or updated advice may be needed.
Valuation.referral: Valuation uncertainty means the value might be wrong.
referralWhy: Uncertainty does not mean the valuation is wrong — it means reduced confidence due to market evidence or asset-specific factors
challenge: What might cause valuation uncertainty?
How would you report uncertainty?
Does uncertainty mean negligence?
How would you explain uncertainty to a lender or client?
keyPoints: Valuation uncertainty affects confidence not necessarily correctness
It should be reported clearly
The client must understand the impact
Evidence limitations should be explained

Valuation.q: What are the main valuation methods?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this to check whether candidates understand the main valuation approaches and can select the right method for the property and purpose — they want to see understanding of application not just a list.
Valuation.pass: The main valuation methods include the comparable method, investment method, profits method, residual method and depreciated replacement cost. The comparable method is used where there is good transactional evidence. The investment method is used for income-producing property. The residual method is often used for development land. The profits method may be used for trading assets and depreciated replacement cost may be used for specialised properties.
Valuation.high: The main valuation methods are selected according to the property type, purpose of valuation and available evidence. The comparable method is used where there is reliable evidence of similar transactions such as residential sales or occupational lettings. The investment method is used for income-producing property where value is derived from rental income, lease terms, risk and yield. The residual method is used for development sites where value is derived from gross development value less costs, finance and developer's profit. The profits method is used for certain trading-related properties where value is linked to maintainable operating profit such as hotels or leisure assets. Depreciated replacement cost may be used for specialised properties where there is limited market evidence. In practice I would select the method most appropriate to the asset and cross-check where possible.
Valuation.referral: The main methods are comparable, investment, residual and profits.
referralWhy: Lists methods but does not explain when or why they are used
challenge: When would you use the investment method?
When would you use the residual method?
Why is DRC sometimes described as a method of last resort?
How would evidence availability affect method selection?
keyPoints: Method selection depends on property purpose and evidence
Comparable evidence underpins many valuations
Income-producing property often requires the investment method
Development valuation is sensitive and should be handled carefully

Valuation.q: How do you ensure a valuation is properly researched and evidenced?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because valuation is about providing properly researched advice — they want to know whether the candidate understands evidence, inspection, analysis and audit trail.
Valuation.pass: I would research relevant comparable evidence, inspect the property, review lease and title information where relevant, confirm floor areas, assess condition and location, and record the assumptions and evidence used. I would then analyse the evidence and make appropriate adjustments before reaching my valuation opinion.
Valuation.high: I would ensure a valuation is properly researched by following a structured process from instruction to report. I would confirm the valuation purpose, basis, date, property interest and scope within the terms of engagement. I would then inspect the property recording location, specification, condition, accommodation, occupation, environmental issues, limitations and any factors affecting value. I would gather comparable evidence from reliable sources and assess whether it was genuinely comparable, considering transaction date, location, size, specification, lease terms, incentives, planning and condition. I would analyse and adjust the evidence documenting my reasoning. For income-producing assets I would also review lease terms, passing rent, market rent, lease events, tenant covenant and yield evidence. Finally I would maintain a valuation file with inspection notes, photographs, calculations, evidence, assumptions and reasoning so there is a clear audit trail supporting the final opinion.
Valuation.referral: I would look at comparable evidence and use my judgement.
referralWhy: Does not explain how evidence is gathered verified analysed or recorded
challenge: What makes evidence reliable?
How would you adjust comparable evidence?
What would you record during inspection?
Why is an audit trail important?
keyPoints: Valuation must be researched evidenced and reasoned
Comparable evidence must be analysed not copied
Inspection findings should link to value
A clear valuation file supports professional judgement

Valuation.q: How would you inspect a property for valuation purposes?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether candidates understand that a valuation inspection is purposeful — it should gather information that supports the valuation opinion, identifies risk and records any limitations.
Valuation.pass: I would inspect the property's location, access, accommodation, specification, condition, services, occupation, layout, site boundaries and any factors that may affect value. I would take photographs, make inspection notes, check measurements where required and record any areas I could not inspect.
Valuation.high: Before inspecting I would confirm the valuation purpose, basis of value, property interest and inspection scope within the terms of engagement. During the inspection I would record factors relevant to value, including location, access, site characteristics, accommodation, specification, condition, layout, building services, occupation, tenure indicators, environmental issues, planning context, EPC position where relevant and any visible defects or limitations. I would also consider how the physical characteristics compare with market evidence. If areas were inaccessible I would record the limitation, consider whether it materially affected the valuation and state any relevant assumption in the report.
Valuation.referral: I would visit the property, look around, take photos and make notes.
referralWhy: Does not explain what is being inspected why it matters to value or how limitations would be handled
challenge: What would you record during inspection?
How would inaccessible areas affect your valuation?
What if you identify a serious defect?
How do inspection findings link to comparable evidence?
keyPoints: Valuation inspection supports the valuation opinion
The inspection should be linked to the valuation purpose
Limitations must be recorded
Physical characteristics must be considered against market evidence

Valuation.q: What information would you record during a valuation inspection?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because a valuation must be supported by an adequate inspection record — candidates need to show what information is relevant and why.
Valuation.pass: I would record the property address, location, access, use, accommodation, floor areas, specification, condition, services, occupation, tenure information, site characteristics, photographs, limitations and any matters requiring further investigation.
Valuation.high: During a valuation inspection I would record enough information to support the valuation conclusion and demonstrate my reasoning. This would include the address, location, surrounding uses, access, visibility, site characteristics, building age, construction, accommodation, layout, specification, condition, services, occupation, lease or tenancy indicators, floor areas, planning use, EPC information, environmental factors, defects, limitations and any matters requiring specialist advice. I would also record market-facing observations — for example whether the property is modern or dated, whether the layout is efficient, whether the specification meets occupier expectations and whether there are factors that would affect demand or yield. The inspection record should be retained in the valuation file with photographs, measurements, notes and any assumptions made.
Valuation.referral: I would record the size, condition and take photos.
referralWhy: Only a small part of the inspection record
Does not show a structured valuation approach
challenge: Why are photographs useful?
What market-facing observations would you record?
How would you record limitations?
How would your inspection differ for a lending valuation?
keyPoints: Inspection notes should support the valuation opinion
Record both physical facts and value-relevant observations
Limitations and assumptions must be documented
A good inspection file protects the client and valuer

Valuation.q: How would you measure a property for valuation purposes?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because measurement affects valuation directly — incorrect measurement can materially affect rental value, capital value and professional liability.
Valuation.pass: I would measure using the appropriate measurement basis for the property type and valuation purpose. For example commercial property may be measured on a Net Internal Area, Gross Internal Area or Gross External Area basis depending on the asset and market convention. I would record the basis used and retain measurement notes.
Valuation.high: I would first identify the correct measurement basis for the property type, purpose of valuation and market convention. For example offices and shops are often analysed by Net Internal Area, industrial property may commonly be analysed by Gross Internal Area, and some development or building-cost contexts may require Gross External Area. I would measure in accordance with the relevant professional measurement standard and record clearly what basis had been used. If I relied on areas provided by another party I would state the source and consider whether verification was required. Measurement must be consistent with the comparable evidence — if my subject property is measured on a different basis from the comparables the analysis may be unreliable. Where measurement was limited I would record the limitation and explain the assumption or reliance in the report.
Valuation.referral: I would measure the property and calculate the floor area.
referralWhy: Does not explain the measurement basis standards accuracy or reporting
challenge: What is the difference between NIA GIA and GEA?
Which basis would you use for an office?
Which basis would you use for an industrial unit?
Why must measurement basis match the comparables?
keyPoints: Measurement affects value
The correct basis depends on property type purpose and market convention
Measurement must be consistent with comparable evidence
Reliance and limitations should be recorded

Valuation.q: What makes comparable evidence reliable?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because valuation depends heavily on evidence — candidates must judge evidence quality not just collect comparables.
Valuation.pass: Reliable comparable evidence should be recent, relevant, verified and similar to the subject property in terms of location, size, specification, condition, use, lease terms and transaction date. Completed transactions usually carry more weight than asking prices or informal market opinion.
Valuation.high: Reliable comparable evidence should be relevant, verified and capable of meaningful comparison with the subject property. I would consider whether the transaction was recent, arm's-length, properly marketed and reflective of market conditions at the valuation date. I would also assess similarities and differences in location, size, specification, condition, tenure, lease terms, incentives, covenant, planning, lot size and date of transaction. Completed open market transactions usually carry stronger weight than asking prices or unverified agent opinion. However where evidence is limited I may consider weaker evidence but clearly explain the weight I have placed on it. I would also adjust or interpret evidence rather than apply it blindly — the key is to understand why the comparable achieved its price or rent and how that relates to the subject property.
Valuation.referral: Reliable evidence is recent evidence from similar properties.
referralWhy: Does not explain comparability verification transaction basis or adjustments
challenge: Would you rely on asking prices?
How would you verify a comparable?
How would you adjust evidence for size?
Why does transaction date matter?
keyPoints: Evidence quality matters
Comparable evidence must be verified and analysed
Completed transactions usually carry more weight
Adjustments require professional judgement

Valuation.q: How would you adjust comparable evidence?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether candidates can interpret evidence and apply professional judgement — valuation is not simply averaging comparables.
Valuation.pass: I would adjust comparable evidence for differences such as location, size, specification, condition, lease terms, transaction date, incentives, tenure and market conditions. The aim is to make the comparable more directly relevant to the subject property.
Valuation.high: I would adjust comparable evidence by first understanding the transaction and then comparing it carefully with the subject property. I would consider location, size, configuration, specification, condition, age, lease terms, incentives, tenant covenant, tenure, planning use, lot size and transaction date. I would also consider market movement between the evidence date and valuation date. The adjustment may be quantitative where there is enough evidence such as applying a rate per square metre or adjusting for rent-free periods. In other cases the adjustment may be qualitative requiring professional judgement. I would not make arbitrary adjustments — I would explain my reasoning and retain the evidence in the valuation file. If the adjustment was material I would make sure the client understood the sensitivity of the valuation.
Valuation.referral: I would adjust the comparable if it was better or worse than the subject property.
referralWhy: Does not explain what factors require adjustment or how the judgement is made
challenge: How would you adjust for incentives?
How would you adjust for size?
What is a qualitative adjustment?
How would you explain adjustments in your report?
keyPoints: Comparable evidence usually needs interpretation
Adjustments should be evidence-led and reasoned
Not all adjustments can be precise
The valuation file should show the reasoning

Valuation.q: How would you deal with limited comparable evidence?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because real valuation instructions often involve imperfect evidence — candidates must act professionally where evidence is weak or limited.
Valuation.pass: If comparable evidence was limited I would widen my search area, review older transactions, consider similar property types, speak to market agents and consider asking prices or under-offers with caution. I would explain the limitations in my valuation report.
Valuation.high: If comparable evidence was limited I would first understand why — the property may be specialised, the market may be thin, or there may have been limited recent transactions. I would then widen the evidence base in a controlled way, considering a wider geography, older evidence adjusted for market movement, similar property types, active market listings, under-offers, agent intelligence and alternative valuation methods or cross-checks. I would assess the reliability of each evidence source and place appropriate weight on it. I would also explain the uncertainty to the client — limited evidence does not prevent a valuation but it can reduce confidence in the conclusion. If material I would report valuation uncertainty and explain any sensitivity around key assumptions.
Valuation.referral: I would use whatever evidence I could find.
referralWhy: Does not explain evidence hierarchy limitations judgement or reporting
challenge: Would you rely on asking prices?
How would you use agent opinion?
When would you use a cross-check?
How would you report uncertainty?
keyPoints: Limited evidence requires careful judgement
Weaker evidence can be used but should be weighted appropriately
Uncertainty should be communicated clearly
Cross-checks can support the valuation opinion

Valuation.q: How do lease terms affect valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because commercial property value is often driven by lease income, risk and lease obligations — the same building can have different values depending on the lease structure.
Valuation.pass: Lease terms can affect valuation through passing rent, rent review provisions, lease length, break clauses, repairing obligations, service charge arrangements, permitted use and tenant covenant. These factors influence income security, risk and marketability.
Valuation.high: Lease terms can materially affect valuation because they determine the nature, duration and risk of the income stream. For an investment property I would review passing rent, market rent, lease expiry, break options, rent review provisions, repairing obligations, alienation clauses, user clauses, service charge, incentives and tenant covenant. A long lease to a strong tenant may support a lower yield and higher capital value while a short lease with a weak covenant or imminent break may increase risk and reduce value. Lease terms also affect rental valuation — Market Rent must be considered on assumed lease terms and comparable evidence should be adjusted where lease terms differ. In practice I would review the lease documents, summarise key terms and consider how each term affects income, risk and market evidence.
Valuation.referral: Lease terms affect valuation because they affect the rent.
referralWhy: Lease terms affect income security risk yield marketability and liabilities
challenge: Why do break clauses affect value?
How does tenant covenant affect yield?
What is the difference between passing rent and market rent?
How can repairing obligations affect value?
keyPoints: Lease terms affect income risk and value
Valuers must review lease documentation carefully
Investment value is strongly linked to lease profile
Rental comparables must be adjusted for lease differences

Valuation.q: How does tenant covenant affect valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because covenant strength affects income security and therefore investor demand, yield and capital value — candidates must connect tenant risk to valuation judgement.
Valuation.pass: Tenant covenant affects valuation because it influences the security of rental income. A financially strong tenant is generally lower risk and may support a sharper yield. A weaker tenant may increase risk and lead to a higher yield or lower value.
Valuation.high: Tenant covenant affects valuation because investors are buying an income stream as well as the underlying property. A strong covenant tenant with good financial standing and a reliable payment history provides greater income security and may make the asset more attractive to investors supporting a lower yield and higher capital value. A weak covenant tenant may increase the risk of arrears, default, insolvency or vacancy — I may reflect the risk through yield selection, purchaser demand, void assumptions or sensitivity analysis. I would assess covenant by reviewing financial accounts, credit reports, payment history, sector risk, parent company support, rent deposits or guarantees. I would not assume that a well-known brand is automatically a strong covenant.
Valuation.referral: A strong tenant makes the property worth more.
referralWhy: Does not explain why or how covenant affects yield and risk
challenge: How would you assess covenant strength?
Does a national brand always mean strong covenant?
How does covenant affect yield?
What is a rent deposit?
keyPoints: Covenant affects income security
Income security affects investor demand and yield
Covenant should be evidenced not assumed
Tenant strength should be considered alongside lease length and market demand

Valuation.q: How would you value a property subject to a lease?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether candidates can value income-producing property — they want to see whether the candidate understands passing rent, market rent, lease terms and yield.
Valuation.pass: I would review the lease, passing rent, lease length, rent review provisions, break options, tenant covenant and repairing obligations. I would compare the passing rent to market rent and then apply an appropriate yield based on investment evidence.
Valuation.high: For a property subject to a lease I would usually apply an investment method depending on the purpose and property type. I would first review the lease to confirm the property interest, tenant, passing rent, lease term, expiry date, break options, rent review provisions, repairing obligations, service charge, alienation and user clauses. I would then compare passing rent with Market Rent to determine whether the property is rack-rented, reversionary or over-rented. I would assess tenant covenant, lease length, income security, future lease events and market demand. I would select an appropriate yield based on comparable investment evidence adjusted for risk factors such as location, covenant, lease term, property quality and market sentiment. Where relevant I would reflect voids, purchaser's costs, rent-free periods, reversionary potential or over-renting risk in the valuation.
Valuation.referral: I would value it based on the rent and apply a yield.
referralWhy: Does not explain lease review income analysis market rent risk or evidence
challenge: What does rack-rented mean?
What does reversionary mean?
How would you treat an over-rented property?
How would you select the yield?
keyPoints: Leased property value depends on income and risk
Passing rent should be compared with Market Rent
Lease terms and covenant affect yield
Investment valuation requires evidence and judgement

Valuation.q: How would you maintain a valuation file?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because a valuation file supports the professional opinion and protects the valuer if the valuation is reviewed, audited or challenged.
Valuation.pass: I would keep the terms of engagement, inspection notes, photographs, measurement records, comparable evidence, calculations, assumptions, correspondence, lease information and a copy of the final report. This provides an audit trail for the valuation.
Valuation.high: I would maintain a clear valuation file that allows another competent valuer to understand how I reached my conclusion. The file would include the terms of engagement, conflict checks, client instructions, property information, title or lease documents where relevant, inspection notes, photographs, measurements, comparable evidence, market research, calculations, assumptions, special assumptions, limitations, correspondence, internal review notes and the final report. I would also record the reasoning behind key judgements such as comparable selection, adjustments, yield choice, rental value opinion or treatment of uncertainty. The file is important because valuation advice may be relied upon by clients and third parties — a clear audit trail demonstrates that the opinion was properly researched, reasoned and prepared in accordance with professional standards.
Valuation.referral: I would keep my notes and the final report.
referralWhy: A valuation file should contain enough evidence to explain and defend the valuation conclusion
challenge: Why is an audit trail important?
What should be retained in a valuation file?
How would you record your comparable analysis?
Who should be able to understand the file?
keyPoints: A valuation file should support the opinion
It should show evidence reasoning and assumptions
Good records protect the client and valuer
Another competent valuer should be able to follow the audit trail

Valuation.q: How would you use the comparable method of valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because the comparable method is one of the most widely used valuation approaches — comparable valuation is not simply averaging evidence but requires selection, verification, analysis and professional judgement.
Valuation.pass: I would use comparable evidence from similar properties that have recently sold or let in the same or similar market. I would compare the evidence against the subject property considering location, size, specification, condition, date of transaction, tenure and lease terms. I would then adjust the evidence where necessary before forming my valuation opinion.
Valuation.high: I would use the comparable method by identifying recent, relevant and verified transactions that are genuinely comparable to the subject property. I would first confirm the valuation basis and purpose then inspect the subject property and understand its characteristics including location, size, specification, condition, tenure, lease terms, planning use and marketability. I would then analyse comparable evidence considering whether each transaction was arm's-length, properly marketed and reflective of market conditions at the valuation date. I would adjust for differences such as location, size, specification, condition, incentives, lease terms and transaction date. I would place most weight on the best evidence and less weight on weaker or less direct evidence. My final valuation would be a reasoned opinion not a mechanical average.
Valuation.referral: I would look at similar properties that have sold or let and use those figures to value the property.
referralWhy: Shows basic awareness but does not explain evidence quality adjustments valuation basis or professional judgement
challenge: What makes a comparable reliable?
Would you use asking prices?
How would you adjust for size or location?
Why should you not simply average comparables?
keyPoints: Comparable valuation requires evidence analysis
Completed verified transactions usually carry more weight
Adjustments should be reasoned and recorded
The final valuation is a professional judgement

Valuation.q: How would you use the investment method of valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether candidates understand income-producing property — how income, lease terms, risk and yield combine to form value.
Valuation.pass: I would use the investment method for an income-producing property. I would review the lease, passing rent, lease length, rent review provisions, break clauses and tenant covenant. I would compare the passing rent with market rent and apply an appropriate yield based on investment evidence.
Valuation.high: I would use the investment method where the property value is driven by an income stream. I would first review the lease documentation to confirm the tenant, passing rent, lease length, rent review provisions, expiry date, break options, repairing obligations and any incentives or side agreements. I would also assess tenant covenant and the security of the income. I would compare the passing rent with Market Rent to determine whether the property is rack-rented, reversionary or over-rented. I would then select an appropriate yield using comparable investment evidence adjusted for location, covenant, lease length, property quality, market sentiment and risk. Where required I would reflect future rent reviews, reversionary income, void periods, rent-free periods, purchaser's costs or over-renting risk. My valuation would explain the income assumptions, yield selection and sensitivity of the result to key variables.
Valuation.referral: I would take the rent and multiply it by a yield.
referralWhy: Does not explain income analysis lease review market rent risk or evidence
challenge: What is passing rent?
How do you select a yield?
What does reversionary mean?
How would you treat an over-rented property?
keyPoints: Investment valuation is income and risk driven
Lease analysis is essential
Yield reflects risk and market evidence
Passing rent and Market Rent must be compared

Valuation.q: What is yield and why does it matter in valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because yield is fundamental to investment valuation — candidates must understand yield as a reflection of return and risk not just a formula.
Valuation.pass: Yield is a measure of return from an investment property. It shows the relationship between income and capital value. In simple terms initial yield can be calculated by dividing annual rent by capital value. Yield matters because it affects the capital value of income-producing property.
Valuation.high: Yield represents the relationship between income, value and risk. In a simple investment the initial yield is calculated by dividing the current annual rent by the capital value. However in practice different yield measures may be relevant such as initial yield, reversionary yield and equivalent yield. Yield matters because it has a direct impact on capital value — if income remains constant a lower yield produces a higher value while a higher yield produces a lower value. The yield selected should reflect market evidence and risk factors including location, tenant covenant, lease length, rent review pattern, property quality, sector demand, liquidity and wider economic conditions. When advising a client I would explain that yield is not just a calculation — it reflects investor perception of risk and return.
Valuation.referral: Yield is the rent divided by the value.
referralWhy: Gives a basic calculation but does not explain what yield represents or how it affects valuation
challenge: What happens to value if yields move out?
How does tenant covenant affect yield?
What is equivalent yield?
Why might a secondary asset attract a higher yield?
keyPoints: Yield reflects return and risk
Yield and capital value move inversely
Yield selection must be evidence-based
Lease and covenant strength strongly affect yield

Valuation.q: How would you use the residual method of valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because residual valuation is commonly used for development land — candidates must understand both the method and its sensitivity.
Valuation.pass: The residual method is used to value development land or property with development potential. I would calculate the gross development value, then deduct construction costs, professional fees, finance, contingency, planning costs, marketing costs and developer's profit. The remaining figure represents the residual land value.
Valuation.high: I would use the residual method where the value of the site is derived from its development potential. The process begins by estimating the gross development value based on the completed scheme and supported by market evidence. I would then deduct all relevant development costs including construction costs, professional fees, finance, contingency, planning obligations, marketing costs, acquisition costs and developer's profit. The residual amount represents the land value. However the residual method is highly sensitive to changes in inputs — small changes in sales values, rents, build costs, finance rates or programme can have a significant impact on the residual value. For that reason I would test sensitivities, explain assumptions clearly and avoid presenting the result as overly precise. I would also consider whether another valuation method or market evidence could be used as a cross-check.
Valuation.referral: I would take the completed value and deduct the development costs.
referralWhy: Does not explain gross development value costs profit finance risk or sensitivity
challenge: What is gross development value?
What costs would you deduct?
Why is residual valuation sensitive?
How would you test your assumptions?
keyPoints: Residual valuation is used for development potential
It is highly sensitive to assumptions
GDV and costs must be evidence-based
Sensitivity analysis is important

Valuation.q: What is the profits method of valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether candidates understand how certain trading properties are valued where value is linked to business performance.
Valuation.pass: The profits method is used for certain trading properties where there is limited direct comparable evidence and value is linked to the property's ability to generate profit. Examples may include hotels, pubs, leisure properties and some healthcare assets.
Valuation.high: The profits method is used where the property is normally bought and sold by reference to its trading potential rather than by direct comparison with similar vacant property. It is commonly used for trading-related assets such as hotels, pubs, cinemas, care homes or leisure facilities where the property's value is linked to maintainable operating profit. The method usually involves assessing the fair maintainable trade, deducting operating costs to establish maintainable operating profit, and then applying an appropriate multiplier or yield depending on the valuation approach and asset type. I would be careful to distinguish the value of the property interest from the value of the business itself, fixtures, goodwill or personal management skill where relevant. I would also review trading accounts critically and consider whether the reported profit is sustainable.
Valuation.referral: The profits method is when you value a property based on profit.
referralWhy: Does not explain when the method applies or how it works
challenge: When would you use the profits method?
What is fair maintainable trade?
How do you distinguish property value from business value?
What risks arise when using the profits method?
keyPoints: The profits method is used for trading-related properties
It relies on maintainable trading performance
Property value and business value must be distinguished
Accounts should be reviewed carefully

Valuation.q: What is depreciated replacement cost?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because DRC is used for specialised properties where there is limited or no direct market evidence — candidates must understand when it is used and its limitations.
Valuation.pass: Depreciated replacement cost is a valuation method used for specialised properties where there is little or no direct market evidence. It estimates the cost of replacing the asset with a modern equivalent and then makes deductions for depreciation, obsolescence and physical deterioration.
Valuation.high: Depreciated replacement cost is a valuation method generally used for specialised properties that are rarely sold in the open market meaning there is limited comparable evidence. The method involves estimating the cost of constructing a modern equivalent asset then deducting for physical deterioration, functional obsolescence and economic obsolescence where appropriate. It is often used for assets such as schools, hospitals, specialist public sector buildings or infrastructure-type assets depending on the instruction and valuation purpose. I would be careful to explain that DRC is not simply the cost of rebuilding the existing asset — it is based on a modern equivalent asset that provides the same service potential. I would also explain the limitations of the method and where possible cross-check against market evidence or sense-check the conclusion.
Valuation.referral: DRC is valuing a property based on what it would cost to rebuild it less depreciation.
referralWhy: Partly correct but does not explain specialised property modern equivalent asset or limitations
challenge: When would you use DRC?
What is a modern equivalent asset?
What types of depreciation may be considered?
Why is DRC sometimes described as a method of last resort?
keyPoints: DRC is used for specialised assets with limited market evidence
It is based on modern equivalent replacement cost
Depreciation and obsolescence must be considered
The method has limitations and should be explained clearly

Valuation.q: How would you value a vacant commercial property?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because vacant commercial property requires judgement around Market Rent, letting prospects, incentives and investor risk — vacancy affects both income and risk.
Valuation.pass: I would assess the Market Rent using comparable rental evidence and consider the likely letting period, tenant demand, incentives, void costs and property condition. If valuing for investment purposes I would reflect the vacancy risk and future income potential in the valuation.
Valuation.high: For a vacant commercial property I would first consider the valuation purpose and basis then inspect the property and assess its marketability. I would estimate Market Rent using comparable evidence adjusted for location, size, specification, condition, lease terms and incentives. I would then consider the likely letting period, occupier demand, void costs, business rates, service charge shortfalls, marketing costs and any works required to make the property lettable. If valuing the property as an investment I would reflect the risk that income is not immediate through a void period, rent-free incentive, letting costs and an appropriate yield once income is assumed. The valuation should explain the assumptions around letting, timing and income risk because they can materially affect value.
Valuation.referral: I would value it based on what rent it could achieve.
referralWhy: Ignores letting period incentives void costs market demand and investment risk
challenge: How would you estimate the letting period?
What void costs might arise?
How do incentives affect Market Rent?
How would you reflect vacancy in an investment valuation?
keyPoints: Vacancy affects both income and risk
Letting assumptions must be realistic
Incentives and void costs can materially affect value
Marketability should be assessed carefully

Valuation.q: How would you value an over-rented property?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether candidates understand the difference between passing rent and Market Rent — an over-rented property can appear attractive because of high income but that income may not be sustainable.
Valuation.pass: An over-rented property is one where the passing rent is above Market Rent. I would value the current income for the period it is secure but reflect the risk that the rent may fall to market level at review, lease expiry or tenant break.
Valuation.high: In an over-rented property the passing rent exceeds Market Rent creating valuation risk because the current income may not be sustainable beyond the secure lease period. I would review the lease carefully including expiry date, break clauses, rent review provisions, security of income and tenant covenant. If the rent is fixed until expiry the over-rent may have value for the remaining term provided the tenant is likely to continue paying. However at lease expiry or relevant lease event I would assess the likelihood of the rent reverting to Market Rent — I may value the term income separately and then value the reversion at Market Rent applying an appropriate yield to reflect the risk. I would also consider whether the over-rented position increases tenant default risk particularly if the tenant is paying significantly above market level.
Valuation.referral: I would value it using the current rent because that is what the landlord receives.
referralWhy: Ignores the risk that the rent may fall at lease expiry or review
Treats income as permanently secure without analysis
challenge: What does over-rented mean?
How would you value the term and reversion?
What if there is a break option?
Could an over-rented property be riskier than a rack-rented one?
keyPoints: Over-rent may not be sustainable
Lease terms determine how long income is secure
Reversion to Market Rent must be considered
Tenant covenant and affordability matter

Valuation.q: How would you value a reversionary property?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because reversionary properties are common in commercial valuation — candidates must understand future rental growth and the relationship between passing rent and Market Rent.
Valuation.pass: A reversionary property is one where the passing rent is below Market Rent. I would value the current income and then reflect the potential increase to Market Rent at the next rent review, lease renewal or expiry depending on the lease terms.
Valuation.high: A reversionary property is one where the current passing rent is below Market Rent creating potential for income growth at a future lease event. I would review the lease to identify when and how the reversion could be captured — at rent review, lease expiry, lease renewal or reletting. I would assess Market Rent using comparable rental evidence and consider the certainty of achieving that rental increase. In valuation terms I may value the current income until the reversion date and then value the reversionary income stream applying yields that reflect the risk and timing of the future increase. I would also test whether the apparent reversion is realistic — a theoretical Market Rent is not enough if the market evidence is weak or the property would require works to achieve it.
Valuation.referral: A reversionary property is worth more because the rent can go up.
referralWhy: Does not explain timing lease events market rent risk or yield
challenge: What does reversionary mean?
How would you identify the reversion date?
How would rent review assumptions affect the value?
How would you reflect risk in the valuation?
keyPoints: Reversionary value depends on future income potential
Lease terms determine when the reversion can be captured
Market Rent must be evidence-based
Future income carries timing and risk considerations

Valuation.q: How would you value development land?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether candidates can apply valuation judgement to development opportunities — understanding planning, gross development value, costs, profit, risk and sensitivity.
Valuation.pass: I would usually use the residual method to value development land. I would estimate the gross development value of the completed scheme, deduct construction costs, professional fees, finance, contingency, planning costs, marketing costs and developer's profit. The residual figure would indicate the land value.
Valuation.high: To value development land I would first confirm the valuation basis, planning status, site constraints and assumed development scheme. I would usually use the residual method supported by comparable land evidence where available. I would estimate the gross development value based on the completed scheme supported by sales or rental evidence. I would then deduct development costs, professional fees, finance, contingency, planning obligations, marketing costs, acquisition costs and developer's profit. Planning status is critical — a site with planning consent may have a different risk profile from one where consent is uncertain. I would also consider abnormal costs, site constraints, build programme, phasing, infrastructure, affordable housing requirements and market demand. Because residual valuation is highly sensitive I would test key assumptions and explain the impact of changes in GDV, build costs, finance rates or profit assumptions. I would also cross-check against land transactions where possible.
Valuation.referral: I would value it using the residual method.
referralWhy: Names a method but does not explain the process inputs risks or evidence
challenge: What is gross development value?
Why is planning status important?
Why is residual valuation sensitive?
How would you cross-check the result?
keyPoints: Development land is often valued using residual method
Planning and site risk materially affect value
Residual valuations are highly sensitive
Cross-checking and sensitivity testing are important

Valuation.q: How would you value a multi-let investment property?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because multi-let assets require more detailed income analysis than a single let property — candidates must analyse the lease profile, income security, void risk, reversionary potential and yield selection.
Valuation.pass: I would review the tenancy schedule, passing rents, lease terms, expiry dates, rent reviews, break options, tenant covenants and any vacant space. I would compare passing rents to Market Rent and apply an appropriate yield based on comparable investment evidence.
Valuation.high: For a multi-let investment property I would begin by reviewing the tenancy schedule and lease documentation for each unit. I would analyse passing rent, Market Rent, lease expiries, break options, rent reviews, tenant covenant strength, arrears, incentives, repairing obligations and any vacant accommodation. I would then consider the income profile of the asset as a whole — assessing whether the property had a long or short WAULT, whether income was diversified across tenants, whether any tenants represented a high proportion of total income, and whether there was reversionary or over-rented income. Vacant units would need separate consideration including likely letting period, rent-free incentives, letting costs, void costs and achievable Market Rent. I would select an appropriate yield or yields based on investment evidence and the risk profile. My valuation would clearly explain the lease assumptions, income analysis, yield selection, void treatment and any sensitivity around future income.
Valuation.referral: I would look at the total rent and apply a yield.
referralWhy: Ignores individual leases voids lease events covenant strength reversionary income and risk
challenge: What is a tenancy schedule?
What is WAULT?
Would you apply one yield to all tenants?
How would tenant concentration affect risk?
keyPoints: Multi-let valuation requires tenant-by-tenant analysis
Income quality matters as much as income amount
Vacancies lease events and covenant strength affect risk
Yield selection should reflect the income profile

Valuation.q: What is WAULT and why does it matter in valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because WAULT is a key investment metric — candidates must understand income duration and how it affects investment risk.
Valuation.pass: WAULT stands for Weighted Average Unexpired Lease Term. It measures the average remaining lease term across a property or portfolio weighted by rental income. It helps investors assess income security and lease event risk.
Valuation.high: WAULT stands for Weighted Average Unexpired Lease Term. It measures the average remaining lease term across an asset or portfolio weighted by income. It matters because it helps investors understand how secure the income stream is and when lease events may occur. A longer WAULT may suggest more secure income provided the tenants have strong covenant strength. A shorter WAULT may indicate higher risk because income could be lost, renegotiated or re-let sooner. It is important to distinguish WAULT to expiry from WAULT to break — if tenants have break options the income may be less secure than the lease expiry dates suggest. In valuation WAULT can influence yield selection, investor appetite and the perceived risk profile of the asset. However it should not be viewed in isolation — covenant strength, rent level, market demand, over-renting, property quality and asset management opportunities also matter.
Valuation.referral: WAULT is the average lease length.
referralWhy: WAULT is weighted by income and can be measured to expiry or break
challenge: How is WAULT calculated?
What is the difference between WAULT to break and WAULT to expiry?
Is a longer WAULT always better?
How does WAULT affect yield?
keyPoints: WAULT measures income duration
It is weighted by rental income
Break options can materially reduce income security
WAULT should be considered alongside covenant and rent sustainability

Valuation.q: How would you assess tenant covenant for valuation purposes?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because covenant strength affects the quality and security of income — candidates must assess tenant risk rather than assume all income is equally secure.
Valuation.pass: I would assess covenant strength by reviewing the tenant's financial accounts, credit rating, payment history, business sector, rent affordability and whether there is a parent company guarantee or rent deposit. A stronger covenant generally supports more secure income and may justify a sharper yield.
Valuation.high: For valuation purposes I would assess tenant covenant as part of the overall income risk profile. I would review financial accounts, credit reports, payment history, sector performance, trading outlook, rent affordability, group structure, guarantees, rent deposits and any recent arrears or concessions. I would not assume covenant strength purely from brand recognition — a well-known tenant may still have weak financials or sector exposure while a smaller tenant may be secure if supported by strong accounts or guarantees. Covenant affects valuation because it influences investor confidence in the income stream — strong covenant income on a long lease may support a lower yield and higher value while weaker covenant income may require a higher yield, greater sensitivity or more cautious assumptions. I would also consider re-letting prospects — if the tenant failed the risk impact would be greater where the property is difficult to re-let.
Valuation.referral: I would check whether the tenant is a good company.
referralWhy: Does not explain how covenant is assessed or how it affects valuation
challenge: Does a national brand always mean strong covenant?
What information would you review?
How does covenant affect yield?
What is a rent deposit?
keyPoints: Covenant strength affects income security
Income security affects investor demand and yield
Covenant should be evidenced not assumed
Re-letting risk should also be considered

Valuation.q: How would you reflect void risk in a valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because void risk affects income, costs and investor appetite — vacancy is not just the absence of rent but creates cost and uncertainty.
Valuation.pass: I would reflect void risk by considering the likely letting period, Market Rent, incentives, letting costs, empty rates, service charge shortfalls and any works needed before occupation. These assumptions would affect the income profile and valuation.
Valuation.high: I would reflect void risk by analysing both the likelihood and financial impact of vacancy. First I would assess market demand for the property considering location, specification, condition, size, EPC position, rent level, competing supply and recent letting evidence. I would then consider the likely void period, rent-free incentive, letting fees, legal fees, empty business rates, service charge shortfalls and any capital expenditure needed to secure a tenant. In an investment valuation I may reflect void risk through explicit deductions, a deferred income approach, a higher yield or sensitivity analysis depending on the valuation method and evidence. I would also consider lease events that may create future void risk such as upcoming expiries or break options. The key is to make assumptions realistic and evidence-based rather than assuming immediate letting.
Valuation.referral: I would reduce the value because the property is empty.
referralWhy: Identifies direction of impact but does not explain how void risk should be analysed or reflected
challenge: What costs arise during a void period?
How would you estimate the letting period?
How do break options create void risk?
How would EPC rating affect void risk?
keyPoints: Void risk affects income and costs
Letting assumptions should be evidence-based
Vacant space may require incentives or capital works
Future void risk should also be considered

Valuation.q: How do break clauses affect valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because break clauses can materially affect income security and therefore value — candidates must understand lease events and income risk.
Valuation.pass: A break clause allows one or both parties to terminate the lease early subject to the lease terms. For valuation purposes a tenant break can reduce income security because the tenant may leave before lease expiry. This can affect WAULT, yield, void assumptions and investment value.
Valuation.high: Break clauses affect valuation because they create uncertainty around the duration of the income stream. I would review the lease to understand who has the benefit of the break, the break date, notice requirements, conditions attached and whether the break is personal to the tenant. I would then assess the likelihood of the break being exercised — considering whether the rent is above or below market, the tenant's occupational requirements, relocation options, fit-out investment, business performance and market availability. If a tenant break is likely or uncertain I may value income to the break date rather than lease expiry or reflect the risk through yield, sensitivity analysis or explicit void assumptions. A break clause does not automatically mean the tenant will leave but it can materially affect investor perception and therefore value.
Valuation.referral: A break clause lets the tenant end the lease early so it can reduce value.
referralWhy: Does not explain likelihood timing conditions tenant motivation or valuation treatment
challenge: What break conditions might apply?
Would you value to break or expiry?
How would you assess likelihood of exercise?
What if the break is personal to the tenant?
keyPoints: Break clauses affect income certainty
The likelihood of exercise should be assessed
Lease wording and conditions matter
Valuation assumptions should be clear

Valuation.q: How do rent reviews affect valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because rent reviews influence future income and investment performance — candidates must understand review mechanisms and their valuation impact.
Valuation.pass: Rent reviews can affect valuation by changing the future rental income. I would review the lease to understand the review date, basis of review, assumptions, disregards and whether the review is upward-only, indexed, fixed or open market.
Valuation.high: Rent reviews affect valuation because they determine how and when the passing rent may change during the lease term. I would review the rent review clause carefully considering the review date, basis, assumptions, disregards, notice requirements, dispute mechanism and whether the review is upward-only, indexed, fixed or open market. If the passing rent is below Market Rent a rent review may create reversionary potential. If the passing rent is above Market Rent an upward-only review may protect the landlord from a rent reduction but the over-rented position may still create tenant affordability or future lease renewal risk. Indexed reviews may provide more predictable income but expose parties to inflation assumptions, caps and collars. In valuation I would reflect the timing, certainty and likely outcome of rent reviews in the income profile and yield selection.
Valuation.referral: Rent reviews affect valuation because the rent may go up.
referralWhy: Rent reviews can operate in different ways and may not always produce an increase depending on the lease terms
challenge: What is an upward-only rent review?
What are assumptions and disregards?
How does an indexed review work?
What if the review is in dispute?
keyPoints: Rent reviews affect future income
The lease clause controls the review mechanism
Different review types carry different risks
Timing and certainty should be reflected in valuation

Valuation.q: How would you value a property with a short unexpired lease term?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because short lease terms can significantly affect income security, investor demand and value — candidates must assess lease expiry risk and future occupation assumptions.
Valuation.pass: I would assess the remaining lease term, tenant covenant, passing rent, Market Rent, likelihood of renewal, market demand and potential void risk. A short lease may increase risk and affect yield but it could also create opportunity if the rent is below market or the property can be re-let at a higher level.
Valuation.high: For a property with a short unexpired lease term I would first assess the security and sustainability of the current income. I would review the lease expiry date, tenant covenant, passing rent compared with Market Rent, renewal rights, tenant intentions, condition of the property, market demand and likely re-letting prospects. If the tenant is likely to vacate I would reflect void period, incentives, letting costs, potential capital expenditure and reletting risk. If renewal is likely I would consider the likely renewal rent and terms. A short lease may reduce value because income certainty is limited and investors may require a higher yield. However it may also create an opportunity where the property is under-rented, capable of refurbishment or suitable for redevelopment. My valuation would clearly state whether I have assumed renewal, reletting or vacancy and explain the evidence supporting that assumption.
Valuation.referral: A short lease makes the property less valuable.
referralWhy: A short lease may reduce income security but may also create reversionary or asset management opportunity
challenge: How would you assess whether the tenant will renew?
How does a short lease affect yield?
Could a short lease increase value?
How would security of tenure affect your assumptions?
keyPoints: Short lease terms create income uncertainty
They can also create asset management opportunity
Valuation depends on market demand and lease assumptions
Renewal or reletting assumptions must be clear

Valuation.q: How would you assess over-renting and under-renting?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether candidates can compare passing rent with Market Rent and understand the valuation implications — essential for investment valuation and lease advisory work.
Valuation.pass: I would assess over-renting or under-renting by comparing the passing rent under the lease with my opinion of Market Rent. If passing rent is above Market Rent the property is over-rented. If passing rent is below Market Rent it is under-rented or reversionary.
Valuation.high: To assess over-renting or under-renting I would compare the passing rent with an evidence-based Market Rent opinion. I would review the lease terms, property specification, location, size, condition and relevant rental comparables. I would also consider incentives and lease assumptions when assessing Market Rent. If the property is over-rented I would consider how long the above-market income is secure, tenant covenant strength, affordability and risk of default or lease event adjustment — I may value the secure term income separately from the reversion to Market Rent. If the property is under-rented I would assess when the reversion can be captured such as at rent review, lease expiry or reletting and consider whether lease terms, market demand or works required could affect the ability to achieve Market Rent. The valuation impact depends on timing, risk and lease structure.
Valuation.referral: Over-rented means rent is too high and under-rented means rent is too low.
referralWhy: Does not explain how the position is assessed or reflected in valuation
challenge: What evidence supports your Market Rent opinion?
How would over-renting affect yield?
How would under-renting create reversionary value?
How does tenant covenant affect over-rented income?
keyPoints: Over-renting and under-renting are assessed against Market Rent
Lease terms determine when income can change
Over-renting creates sustainability risk
Under-renting may create reversionary potential

Valuation.q: How would economic conditions influence valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because valuation is market-facing — candidates must understand how wider economic conditions influence demand, yields, rents and investor behaviour.
Valuation.pass: Economic conditions can influence valuation through interest rates, inflation, occupier demand, investor sentiment, finance availability, construction costs, rental growth and yields. These factors can affect both income and capital value.
Valuation.high: Economic conditions influence valuation through their effect on occupier demand, investor demand, finance costs, rental growth expectations and risk perception. For example higher interest rates may reduce investor demand or lead investors to require higher yields which can reduce capital values. Inflation may affect operating costs, construction costs and indexed rent reviews. Weak economic growth may reduce occupier demand, increase void risk and limit rental growth. However the impact is not uniform — prime assets with secure income may be more resilient while secondary assets, short-income properties or development sites may be more exposed. In practice I would consider current market evidence rather than making broad assumptions — analysing comparable transactions, investor sentiment, leasing activity, yield movement and sector-specific conditions before reflecting economic factors in my valuation.
Valuation.referral: If the economy is bad values go down.
referralWhy: Economic conditions affect different sectors and assets in different ways
challenge: How do interest rates affect yields?
How can inflation affect rental income?
Are all property sectors affected equally?
How would economic uncertainty be reported?
keyPoints: Economic conditions affect income risk and yield
Impacts differ by sector and asset quality
Market evidence remains essential
Valuation should reflect evidence not headlines

Valuation.q: How would you advise a client where valuation evidence is uncertain?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because valuers must communicate uncertainty responsibly — candidates must explain limitations without undermining the valuation or misleading the client.
Valuation.pass: I would explain that the evidence is limited or uncertain and that this affects the confidence level of the valuation. I would record the limitations in the report and if appropriate recommend further evidence, sensitivity analysis or an updated valuation when more evidence becomes available.
Valuation.high: Where valuation evidence is uncertain I would explain the nature, cause and potential impact of that uncertainty to the client. For example uncertainty may arise because there are few recent transactions, the property is specialised, market conditions are changing quickly, or the available evidence is indirect or unverified. I would still provide a valuation opinion if it was within my competence and the evidence was sufficient to do so but I would explain the degree of confidence attached to the conclusion. I would avoid generic caveats and instead identify the specific evidence limitations and how I have treated them. Where appropriate I would provide sensitivity analysis, cross-check using another method, recommend further information, or advise that the valuation should be reviewed after a key event or once more market evidence becomes available. The aim is to help the client understand how much reliance can reasonably be placed on the valuation in the circumstances.
Valuation.referral: I would tell the client the valuation may not be accurate.
referralWhy: Valuation uncertainty does not automatically mean the valuation is inaccurate
challenge: What causes valuation uncertainty?
Does uncertainty mean you should not value?
When would sensitivity analysis be useful?
How would you avoid misleading the client?
keyPoints: Uncertainty affects confidence not necessarily correctness
Clients need clear explanation of evidence limitations
Sensitivity analysis may help
Valuers should communicate uncertainty honestly and proportionately

Valuation.q: Tell us about your valuation case study.
Valuation.why: Assessors establish whether the candidate genuinely understands their valuation instruction and can explain their personal role, the client objective, the valuation basis, the evidence relied upon, the advice given and the outcome.
Valuation.pass: My case study involved a valuation instruction for a property where the client required advice for a specific purpose such as acquisition, disposal, secured lending, accounts, taxation or internal decision-making. My role was to inspect the property, review the relevant information, research comparable evidence and assist in preparing the valuation advice. I considered the appropriate valuation method, analysed the evidence and helped produce a valuation report for the client.
Valuation.high: My case study involved a valuation instruction where the client required advice for a specific purpose. My personal role was to review the instruction, confirm the valuation basis and scope, inspect the property, analyse the evidence and provide reasoned valuation advice. The key valuation issue required professional judgement around evidence, methodology, assumptions or uncertainty. I selected the valuation method because it matched the asset type, purpose and available evidence. I analysed the evidence, explained limitations where evidence was imperfect and applied professional judgement. My final advice was appropriate because it was based on the agreed valuation basis, relevant evidence, clear assumptions and a reasoned methodology.
Valuation.referral: My case study was about valuing a property for a client. I inspected it, looked at comparables and prepared the valuation.
referralWhy: Does not explain purpose basis property type evidence methodology personal role or professional judgement
challenge: What was your personal role?
What was the purpose of the valuation?
What basis of value did you use?
What was the main valuation risk?
keyPoints: Case study answers should be structured
Assessors want your valuation reasoning not the whole project history
Your personal role must be clear
The valuation basis method evidence and judgement should all be explained
Valuation.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Valuation.q: What was your personal role in the valuation instruction?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because candidates often describe team activity rather than their own contribution — they need to understand what the candidate personally did, what advice they gave and where they exercised judgement.
Valuation.pass: My personal role was to inspect the property, gather comparable evidence, review the property information and assist in preparing the valuation. I contributed to the analysis by comparing the subject property against market evidence and helping to prepare the valuation file.
Valuation.high: My personal role was to inspect, analyse, value or report on a specific property or element under appropriate supervision. I reviewed the terms of engagement to understand the valuation basis, purpose and scope. I then inspected the property, recorded relevant factors affecting value, reviewed lease or title information where relevant, researched comparable evidence and analysed its reliability. My key contribution was a specific judgement such as selecting the most appropriate comparable evidence, adjusting evidence for lease terms, assessing the yield, considering valuation uncertainty or advising on how limited evidence should be reported. I also prepared or contributed to the valuation file including inspection notes, evidence, calculations, assumptions and reasoning.
Valuation.referral: We inspected the property and prepared the valuation report.
referralWhy: Assessors cannot score competence if the candidate only describes what the team did
challenge: What did you personally inspect?
What evidence did you personally analyse?
What judgement did you make?
What did you learn from the review process?
keyPoints: APC assessors score the candidate's competence
Personal role must be honest and specific
Supervised work can still demonstrate competence
Candidates should explain judgement not just activity
Valuation.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Valuation.q: Why was your valuation method appropriate?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether the candidate understands method selection — the method should match the asset, purpose and available evidence not just be familiar.
Valuation.pass: The method was appropriate because it matched the property type and the evidence available. For example I used the comparable method because there was relevant transactional evidence or the investment method because the property was income-producing.
Valuation.high: The valuation method was appropriate because it reflected the nature of the asset, the purpose of valuation, the basis of value and the evidence available. Where the property was income-producing the investment method was appropriate because value was driven by rental income, lease terms, covenant strength and yield. Where the property had strong comparable transaction evidence the comparable method was appropriate because market participants would rely on similar evidence. I also considered whether a cross-check was needed — for example if using the investment method I may have cross-checked against capital value per square foot or comparable investment transactions. The method was selected because it reflected market behaviour and produced a reasoned valuation opinion supported by evidence.
Valuation.referral: The method was appropriate because it is the standard method for that type of property.
referralWhy: Does not explain the reasoning or link the method to the valuation instruction
challenge: What other methods did you consider?
Why did you reject them?
Did you use a cross-check?
What were the limitations of your chosen method?
keyPoints: Method selection must be justified
The method should reflect asset type purpose and evidence
Cross-checks can strengthen valuation advice
Level 3 candidates explain why the method was suitable
Valuation.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Valuation.q: What evidence did you rely on and why?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because valuation is evidence-led — candidates must explain the quality and relevance of the evidence relied upon.
Valuation.pass: I relied on recent comparable evidence that was similar to the subject property in terms of location, size, specification, condition and transaction date. I gave greater weight to completed and verified transactions than to asking prices or unverified market commentary.
Valuation.high: I relied on evidence that was recent, relevant, verified and comparable to the subject property. I considered completed transactions first because they provide stronger market evidence than asking prices or informal opinion. I then assessed each comparable against the subject property considering location, size, specification, condition, lease terms, incentives, covenant, transaction date and whether the transaction was arm's-length. Where evidence was not directly comparable I adjusted it or placed less weight on it. I also considered the reliability of the evidence source and sought to verify details where possible. My final valuation was based on the strongest evidence supported by professional judgement and a clear explanation of the adjustments made.
Valuation.referral: I relied on comparable evidence from similar properties.
referralWhy: Does not explain which evidence was selected how it was verified or why it was reliable
challenge: Which comparable carried the most weight and why?
How did you verify the evidence?
How did you adjust the evidence?
What evidence did you reject?
keyPoints: Evidence must be selected and analysed
Completed verified transactions usually carry greater weight
Weak evidence can be used cautiously but should be explained
Candidates should know why they relied on each comparable
Valuation.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Valuation.q: What was the greatest valuation risk in your instruction?
Valuation.why: Assessors test whether the candidate understood the main risk within the valuation and how it was managed — looking for professional judgement and risk awareness.
Valuation.pass: The greatest risk was a specific issue such as limited comparable evidence, uncertain lease terms, weak covenant, valuation uncertainty, planning risk or development sensitivity. I managed this by reviewing the evidence carefully, recording assumptions and explaining the limitations in the valuation report.
Valuation.high: The greatest valuation risk was a specific issue that could materially affect the valuation conclusion and the client's reliance on the advice. For example if evidence was limited the risk was that the valuation depended on indirect or weaker comparables — I managed this by widening the evidence base, verifying sources, applying reasoned adjustments and reporting the uncertainty clearly. If the risk related to lease terms I reviewed the lease carefully and considered how break clauses, rent reviews, over-renting or covenant strength affected the income profile. If the risk related to development value I tested sensitivities around GDV, build costs, finance and developer's profit. I explained the risk to the client in a proportionate way and made sure the valuation file clearly recorded my reasoning, assumptions and limitations.
Valuation.referral: The main risk was getting the valuation wrong.
referralWhy: Does not identify the source of the risk or explain how it affected the valuation
challenge: How did you identify the risk?
How did you reflect it in the valuation?
How did you explain it to the client?
What would you do if more evidence became available later?
keyPoints: Valuation risk must be specific
Risk should be linked to value impact
Assumptions and limitations should be recorded
Strong candidates explain how risk was managed
Valuation.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Valuation.q: How did you deal with valuation uncertainty?
Valuation.why: Assessors ask this because valuers must communicate uncertainty clearly and responsibly — candidates must explain uncertainty without undermining the valuation or misleading the client.
Valuation.pass: I identified the source of uncertainty such as limited evidence or market volatility and explained it in the valuation report. I also recorded the assumptions and limitations and advised the client that the valuation should be considered in that context.
Valuation.high: I dealt with valuation uncertainty by identifying its cause, assessing its impact and communicating it clearly to the client. I considered whether I still had enough evidence and competence to provide a valuation then reviewed alternative evidence sources, cross-checked where possible and considered whether sensitivity analysis was appropriate. In the report I avoided generic wording and explained the specific uncertainty, why it mattered and how it could affect reliance on the valuation. I also advised the client on next steps such as reviewing the valuation if further evidence emerged, if lease terms changed or if market conditions moved materially.
Valuation.referral: I told the client the valuation might not be exact.
referralWhy: Does not explain the cause impact or treatment of uncertainty
challenge: What caused the valuation uncertainty?
Did uncertainty prevent you from valuing?
How did you explain it in the report?
What advice did you give the client?
keyPoints: Uncertainty affects confidence not necessarily correctness
It should be specific and clearly explained
Cross-checks and sensitivity analysis may help
The client needs to understand how to rely on the valuation
Valuation.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Valuation.q: How did you protect your client's interests during the valuation?
Valuation.why: Assessors test client care, professional integrity and objectivity — protecting the client means giving objective competent and properly evidenced advice not giving the value they want.
Valuation.pass: I protected the client by agreeing clear terms of engagement, using appropriate evidence, recording assumptions and preparing the valuation in accordance with professional standards. I also explained any limitations or risks in the report.
Valuation.high: I protected my client's interests by ensuring the valuation was objective, properly scoped, evidence-based and suitable for the purpose for which it was required. I began by confirming the terms of engagement including the client, purpose, basis of value, valuation date, scope, assumptions, limitations and reliance. I then carried out appropriate inspection and evidence gathering, analysed the evidence critically and recorded my reasoning in the valuation file. Where there were limitations, uncertainty or assumptions I explained these clearly so the client understood how the valuation could be relied upon. I also maintained professional independence — if the client had an expected value I did not simply adopt it. My duty was to provide an impartial valuation opinion supported by evidence and professional judgement.
Valuation.referral: I protected the client by giving them the best valuation I could.
referralWhy: Does not explain process objectivity evidence or client reliance
challenge: What if the client wanted a higher value?
How did you maintain independence?
Why are terms of engagement important?
How did your advice help the client make a decision?
keyPoints: Client care requires objective advice
Valuations must be suitable for their purpose
Independence protects both client and valuer
