Residential.q: How would you advise a client on dampness in a residential property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because damp is common in residential property and candidates must avoid simplistic diagnosis. They want to hear a structured approach to identifying possible causes, explaining risk and recommending appropriate further investigation.
Residential.pass: I would inspect the property for signs of damp, such as staining, mould, peeling decoration, high moisture readings, salt deposits, defective rainwater goods, bridging of damp-proof course or poor ventilation. I would consider whether the damp may be rising damp, penetrating damp or condensation and recommend further investigation if required.
Residential.high: I would advise the client by explaining that dampness is a symptom, not a diagnosis. I would inspect internally and externally to identify possible causes — externally I would check rainwater goods, roof coverings, flashings, render, pointing, ground levels, damp-proof course position, drainage and external defects, while internally I would look for staining, mould, condensation, salt deposits, damp meter readings, ventilation issues and patterns of damage. I would consider whether the evidence suggested penetrating damp, rising damp, condensation or plumbing leaks, and avoid recommending treatment until the likely cause had been identified. For example, damp at low level may be caused by bridged damp-proof course, high external ground levels or defective drainage rather than true rising damp — black mould in corners may indicate condensation and ventilation problems rather than water ingress. My advice would explain the likely cause, implications for value or repair cost, and whether specialist investigation was needed.
Residential.referral: I would tell the client the property has damp and needs treatment.
referralWhy: Jumps to a conclusion without identifying type or cause
challenge: How would you distinguish rising damp and condensation?
What external defects can cause damp?
Why can damp meters be misleading?
When would you recommend a specialist?
keyPoints: Damp is a symptom, not a diagnosis
External inspection is essential
Different damp types require different remedies
Further investigation may be needed before treatment

Residential.q: How would you assess cracking in a residential property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because cracking can range from minor cosmetic movement to serious structural risk. They want to know whether candidates can assess severity, pattern, cause and appropriate next steps.
Residential.pass: I would assess the crack width, pattern, location, direction, whether it is internal or external, whether there are signs of movement and whether related defects are present. I would consider possible causes such as settlement, thermal movement, lintel failure, subsidence, tree influence or poor alterations.
Residential.high: I would assess cracking by looking at its characteristics and context. I would record the width, direction, pattern, location, whether it is stepped, vertical, horizontal or diagonal, whether it appears old or progressive, and whether there are related signs such as sticking doors, sloping floors, distorted openings or external cracking. I would then consider likely causes — fine plaster cracks may be shrinkage or thermal movement, while stepped cracking through brickwork, distortion around openings or cracking linked to trees and drainage may suggest more significant movement. I would also consider the building's age, construction type, ground conditions, nearby trees, drains, extensions, previous alterations and history of movement. If there was evidence of significant or ongoing movement, I would advise further investigation by a structural engineer or appropriate specialist before the client proceeded.
Residential.referral: I would check whether the cracks are big or small.
referralWhy: Too simplistic — pattern, location, age and cause also matter

When would you recommend a structural engineer?
How could trees affect cracking?
How would cracking affect valuation advice?

Not all cracks are structural
Movement risk should be explained clearly
Serious or uncertain cracking requires specialist advice

Residential.q: What is subsidence and how would you identify possible signs?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because subsidence can materially affect value, insurance, mortgageability and client risk. They want to see whether the candidate can identify warning signs and advise appropriately.
Residential.pass: Subsidence is downward movement of the ground supporting a building, which can cause structural movement. Possible signs include diagonal or stepped cracking, cracks wider at the top, distorted openings, sticking doors or windows, sloping floors and cracking near extensions or trees.
Residential.high: Subsidence is downward movement of the ground beneath a building, causing the foundations and structure to move. It can be caused by factors such as shrinkable clay soil, tree root influence, leaking drains, poor ground conditions, mining, inadequate foundations or changes in groundwater. During inspection I would look for signs such as stepped or diagonal cracking, distortion around doors and windows, tapering cracks, uneven floors, separation between building elements, cracking around extensions and evidence of drainage defects or nearby vegetation. I would not confirm subsidence without appropriate investigation — if suspected, I would recommend further investigation, which may include structural engineer advice, drainage survey, monitoring, soil investigation or arboricultural input. I would also advise the client that suspected or confirmed subsidence may affect value, insurance, mortgageability and future saleability.
Residential.referral: Subsidence is when a house sinks.
referralWhy: Too basic — does not explain cause, symptoms, risk or advice
challenge: What causes subsidence?
How does clay soil affect risk?
Why do trees matter?
How can subsidence affect marketability?
keyPoints: Subsidence is ground movement affecting structure
Signs must be considered in context
Specialist investigation is often required
Subsidence can materially affect value and marketability

Residential.q: How would you advise on roof defects in a residential property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because roof defects are common and can cause significant repair liability and internal damage. They want to know whether candidates can inspect safely, identify likely defects and explain client implications.
Residential.pass: I would inspect the roof from ground level and accessible areas, looking at coverings, ridge tiles, flashings, chimneys, gutters, downpipes, roof structure and signs of leaks internally. I would record limitations and recommend further investigation if defects were suspected but not fully visible.
Residential.high: I would inspect the roof safely and within the agreed survey scope, usually from ground level, accessible windows, loft space where accessible and other safe vantage points. Externally I would look for slipped or missing tiles, defective slates, damaged ridge tiles, failing flashings, chimney defects, poor pointing, sagging roof slopes, blocked gutters, defective rainwater goods and signs of previous patch repairs. Internally I would look for water staining, daylight through coverings, dampness, timber decay, inadequate ventilation, insulation issues, roof spread, structural movement or unauthorised alterations. I would explain to the client whether the defects appear minor, require repair, or may need specialist roofing or structural advice — if the roof could not be fully inspected I would record the limitation and advise accordingly. Roof defects can affect value, future repair cost and immediate occupation risk, particularly where water ingress is active.
Residential.referral: I would check whether the roof looks old or damaged.
referralWhy: Too superficial — does not explain specific roof elements or further investigation

Residential.q: What is Japanese knotweed and why is it relevant to residential property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because Japanese knotweed can affect value, lending, saleability and legal risk. They want to know whether candidates can identify risk and advise further action without overstating their expertise.
Residential.pass: Japanese knotweed is an invasive plant that can affect residential property value and marketability. If suspected, I would advise specialist identification and treatment advice. Its presence may affect mortgageability, insurance, saleability and legal disclosure.
Residential.high: Japanese knotweed is an invasive plant species that can spread quickly and may affect residential property marketability, lender appetite and legal obligations. During inspection I would look for visible signs in the garden, boundaries, neighbouring land and disturbed ground, particularly during the growing season — however I would be cautious because identification can be seasonal and specialist confirmation may be required. If suspected, I would advise the client to obtain specialist advice from an appropriate invasive plant contractor or surveyor. A treatment management plan, insurance-backed guarantee and proper documentation may be relevant to saleability and lending. I would also explain that the issue is not only physical damage — the key residential risks are perception, mortgageability, legal disclosure, potential neighbour issues and future treatment liability.

referralWhy: Too simplistic — does not explain identification, risk, lending or legal implications

Residential.q: How would you advise on non-standard construction?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because non-standard construction can affect value, mortgageability, insurance and repair risk. They want to see whether candidates can recognise unusual construction and advise appropriately.
Residential.pass: Non-standard construction refers to properties not built using traditional brick or block cavity wall construction. Examples may include concrete, timber frame, steel frame, prefabricated or system-built housing. These properties may have mortgageability, insurance, repair or resale issues.
Residential.high: Non-standard construction refers to residential property built using methods or materials outside conventional market expectations, such as precast concrete, steel frame, timber frame, cob, thatch, prefabricated systems or certain post-war system-built houses. The relevance is that some forms of non-standard construction may have known defects, limited lender appetite, specialist repair requirements, insurance issues or reduced buyer demand. During inspection I would try to identify the construction type through visible evidence, age, property records, local authority information, previous surveys or specialist reports — I would not assume the construction type without evidence. My advice would explain the implications for value, marketability, mortgageability, insurance and repair liability. Where construction type was uncertain or specialist risk existed, I would recommend further investigation by an appropriately qualified specialist.

Residential.q: How would you advise on asbestos risk in a residential property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because asbestos may be present in older residential properties and can affect safety, refurbishment, cost and client risk. They want to see whether candidates understand risk awareness and referral.
Residential.pass: If asbestos-containing materials were suspected, I would advise the client that specialist asbestos advice or testing may be required. I would not disturb the material and would explain that asbestos risk depends on condition, location, likelihood of disturbance and future works.
Residential.high: I would advise on asbestos risk by recognising that asbestos may be present in older residential properties, particularly in materials such as textured coatings, floor tiles, soffits, pipe insulation, cement sheets, garage roofs or older service ducts. During inspection I would not disturb suspected materials — if asbestos was suspected or if refurbishment works were planned, I would recommend specialist asbestos survey or testing. The risk depends on whether the material contains asbestos, its condition, whether fibres can be released and whether it is likely to be disturbed — in some cases management in situ may be appropriate, in others removal by specialists may be required. I would explain to the client that asbestos can affect repair costs, refurbishment planning, health and safety duties and marketability, but I would avoid giving specialist asbestos advice beyond my competence.

Residential.q: How would defects affect residential value?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because candidates must connect building condition to value, marketability and client advice. They want to see that candidates understand defects commercially, not just technically.
Residential.pass: Defects can affect residential value by reducing buyer demand, increasing repair costs, affecting mortgageability or creating uncertainty. The impact depends on the type, severity, cost of repair and whether the defect is common or unusual for that property type.
Residential.high: Defects affect residential value through their impact on cost, risk, marketability and buyer confidence. Minor defects may have little or no measurable value impact, especially if they are typical for the property's age and condition. More significant defects, such as structural movement, damp, roof failure, defective services, non-standard construction or Japanese knotweed, may reduce value because they create repair liability, lender concerns or uncertainty. I would assess the likely buyer response and the available evidence — if comparable sales include similar properties in similar condition, the market may already reflect the defect. If the defect is unusual or material, I may need to adjust my valuation or recommend further investigation before final advice. I would be careful not to simply deduct an estimated repair cost pound-for-pound unless market evidence supported that approach — the value impact may be greater or less than the repair cost depending on risk perception and buyer demand.

Residential.q: When would you recommend further investigation?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential surveyors must recognise the limits of inspection and competence. They want to know whether the candidate can identify when a client needs specialist advice before proceeding.
Residential.pass: I would recommend further investigation where there are significant defects, inaccessible areas, suspected structural movement, damp, roof issues, asbestos, Japanese knotweed, drainage problems, non-standard construction or services concerns. This would help the client understand the risk before proceeding.
Residential.high: I would recommend further investigation where the inspection identifies a material issue that cannot be fully assessed within the scope of the survey or my competence, and where that issue could affect value, safety, cost, mortgageability or the client's decision to proceed. Examples include suspected structural movement, significant damp, roof defects, drainage concerns, asbestos, Japanese knotweed, non-standard construction, defective services, boundary issues, unauthorised alterations, fire safety concerns in flats or leasehold documentation issues. I would explain why further investigation is needed, what type of specialist should be instructed and whether the investigation should take place before exchange of contracts. For example, if I observed stepped cracking and distortion around openings, I would recommend structural engineer advice before the client committed to purchase. The advice should be proportionate — further investigation should not be used as a generic caveat, it should be linked to a specific risk.

Residential.q: What key leasehold issues would you consider when advising on a residential flat?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because leasehold flats can carry risks that affect value, mortgageability, saleability and client decision-making. They want to see whether candidates understand leasehold as a major residential risk area, not just a legal detail for solicitors.
Residential.pass: I would consider the unexpired lease term, ground rent, service charge, repairing obligations, reserve fund, management arrangements, restrictions, rights of access, major works, lease extension rights and mortgageability. I would also advise the client to obtain legal advice on the lease terms.
Residential.high: When advising on a residential flat, I would treat the lease as central to the property interest being valued or purchased. I would consider the unexpired lease term, ground rent provisions, service charge level, reserve fund, major works liability, repairing obligations, management structure, rights of access, rights to use communal areas, restrictions on alterations or subletting, insurance arrangements and any known disputes. I would also consider how these issues affect value and marketability — for example, a short lease may reduce mortgageability and buyer demand, a high or uncertain service charge may affect affordability, and planned major works may influence a purchaser's offer or willingness to proceed. I would not provide legal advice beyond my competence, but I would flag material leasehold risks and recommend solicitor or specialist leasehold advice where required.

Residential.q: How would service charges affect residential advice?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because service charges affect affordability, marketability and buyer confidence, especially for flats and managed estates. They want to see whether candidates understand service charge as both a financial and perception issue.
Residential.pass: Service charges are payments made by leaseholders towards the cost of managing, maintaining, repairing and insuring the building or estate. High or uncertain service charges can affect affordability, marketability and buyer demand.
Residential.high: Service charges can materially affect residential advice because they influence both affordability and market perception. I would consider the current annual service charge, what it covers, whether it appears proportionate, whether there is a reserve fund, whether major works are planned, and whether there have been significant increases. For a purchaser, a high service charge may reduce affordability and affect willingness to proceed — for a valuation, it may affect marketability if comparable flats have lower charges or if buyers perceive poor value for money. I would also consider the quality of management — a well-managed building with transparent service charges and a healthy reserve fund may be more attractive than a poorly managed building with unpredictable demands. I would advise the client to obtain full service charge accounts and legal information through their solicitor before exchange.

Residential.q: How would ground rent affect residential value or marketability?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because ground rent can affect buyer appetite, lender requirements and leasehold value. They want to know whether candidates understand that ground rent is not just a small annual payment.
Residential.pass: Ground rent is an annual payment made by the leaseholder to the freeholder under the lease. It can affect value and marketability if it is high, increases significantly over time, or causes lender or buyer concern.
Residential.high: An important threshold distinction applies between new and existing leases. The Leasehold Reform (Ground Rent) Act 2022 prohibits regulated ground rents on new residential leases entered into from 30 June 2022 — new leases must have a peppercorn ground rent only. Ground rent as a substantive financial consideration therefore applies to existing pre-Act leasehold stock. Ground rent can affect residential value and marketability depending on its amount, review mechanism and lender perception. A low fixed ground rent may have limited impact — however, a high ground rent, aggressive review pattern or unusual escalation clause can reduce buyer demand and create mortgageability concerns. When advising, I would review the ground rent amount, review frequency, increase mechanism and any relationship with the property value. I would also consider whether the ground rent terms are typical for the market and whether they may concern lenders or future purchasers. I would not provide legal advice on the enforceability of lease terms, but I would flag the issue and advise the client to seek solicitor advice before exchange.
Residential.referral: Ground rent is a payment made to the freeholder and it can reduce value if it is high.
referralWhy: Partly correct but too limited — does not explain review patterns or lender concerns
Assuming small ground rent is always irrelevant
challenge: Why can ground rent concern lenders?
What is an escalating ground rent?
How would ground rent affect marketability?
What advice would you give the client?
keyPoints: Ground rent terms can affect marketability
Review mechanisms matter
Lender perception is important
Legal advice should be recommended where lease terms are material

Residential.q: How would you advise on planned major works in a residential block?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because major works can create significant financial liability for leaseholders and may affect saleability. They want candidates to understand the practical and valuation implications.
Residential.pass: Major works can affect a leaseholder because they may lead to significant service charge demands. I would advise the client to obtain details of planned works, estimated costs, timing, consultation notices, reserve fund position and leaseholder liability.
Residential.high: Planned major works can materially affect residential advice because they may create a significant future cost and influence buyer demand. I would ask whether works are planned or ongoing, what they relate to, the estimated cost, timing, consultation process, whether a reserve fund exists, and how costs will be apportioned between leaseholders — for example, roof replacement, cladding works, lift replacement, external repairs or communal fire safety works may create substantial liability. From a valuation or purchase advice perspective, I would consider whether the market is already aware of the works, whether comparable evidence reflects similar liability, and whether a purchaser would seek a price adjustment or retention. I would advise the client to obtain full legal and management information before exchange, including managing agent replies, service charge accounts, reserve fund details and any notices relating to major works.
Residential.referral: I would tell the client major works may cost money.

Reserve funds may reduce immediate impact
Buyers may adjust offers where major liability exists

Residential.q: How would you advise a landlord letting a residential property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential lettings involve market advice, tenant suitability, compliance and risk management. They want to see whether candidates can advise landlords responsibly.
Residential.pass: I would advise the landlord on Market Rent, marketing strategy, tenant demand, property presentation, tenant referencing, tenancy terms, deposit requirements, safety obligations and management responsibilities. I would also ensure the landlord understands their legal obligations before letting.
Residential.high: I would advise a landlord by first understanding their objectives, whether they want short-term income, long-term tenant stability, full management or let-only service. I would inspect the property and advise on achievable rent, target tenant profile, presentation, repairs, compliance requirements, safety obligations, deposit protection, tenancy documentation, inventory, referencing and management responsibilities. I would also consider risk — for example, a higher rent may attract interest, but overpricing can increase void periods, a weak tenant referencing process can increase arrears or possession risk, and poor property condition can lead to complaints, enforcement or reputational issues. My advice would aim to help the landlord achieve sustainable rental income while complying with legal requirements and protecting both landlord and tenant interests. Where legal requirements were specific or complex, I would recommend appropriate legal or specialist advice. My advice would be framed by the RICS Real estate management standard, the applicable professional standard setting out obligations and best practice for residential property management, including landlord duties, client money handling, service charge management and statutory compliance.

What safety obligations should landlords consider?
Why is an inventory important?
keyPoints: Lettings advice includes rent, compliance and risk
Tenant referencing protects the landlord
Property condition and safety obligations matter
Sustainable letting is better than simply maximising rent

Residential.q: How would you assess Market Rent for a residential letting?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because candidates need to show they can advise on rental value using evidence, not guesswork. They want to hear how residential rental evidence is gathered and analysed.
Residential.pass: I would assess Market Rent by reviewing comparable rental evidence for similar properties in the area. I would consider property type, size, condition, specification, furnishings, location, outside space, parking, transport links, tenant demand and current competition.
Residential.high: I would assess residential Market Rent by considering recent achieved lettings, current competing stock and tenant demand. I would compare the subject property with similar properties in terms of location, size, accommodation, condition, specification, furnishings, outside space, parking, energy performance, transport links and local amenities. I would place greater weight on achieved rents where available, but I may also consider asking rents and agent market intelligence with caution. I would also consider the landlord's objective — if the landlord wants minimal void and a reliable tenant, I may advise a rent that is competitive rather than overly ambitious, while if the property is highly desirable and demand is strong, a higher asking rent may be justified. The final advice should balance rental level, letting speed, tenant quality and void risk.

Using online asking rents as direct evidence

Residential.q: What checks would you carry out before recommending a tenant?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because tenant selection affects arrears, property condition, compliance and landlord risk. They want candidates to understand referencing and responsible letting practice.
Residential.pass: I would carry out tenant referencing, including identity checks, income or employment checks, credit checks, previous landlord references and right to rent checks where applicable. I would report the results to the landlord so they can make an informed decision.
Residential.high: Before recommending a tenant, I would ensure a fair, consistent and compliant referencing process was followed. This would include identity verification, affordability assessment, employment or income checks, credit history, previous landlord reference, right to rent checks where applicable, and consideration of guarantor requirements where risk exists. I would also consider whether the tenant's proposed use of the property is consistent with the tenancy terms, occupancy limits, licensing requirements and landlord expectations. My advice to the landlord would not simply say 'accept' or 'reject' — I would explain the strength of the application, any risks identified and possible mitigations, such as a guarantor, rent in advance or further verification. I would ensure decisions are made fairly and without unlawful discrimination.

referralWhy: Affordability is important but too narrow — tenant suitability requires broader checks

How would you avoid discrimination?
keyPoints: Tenant selection should be evidence-based
Referencing protects landlord and tenant
Fairness and compliance matter
Risks can sometimes be mitigated

Residential.q: Why is an inventory important in residential lettings?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because inventories are crucial in managing deposit disputes and property condition. They want to see whether candidates understand evidence, fairness and dispute prevention.
Residential.pass: An inventory records the contents and condition of the property at the start of the tenancy. It is important because it provides evidence if there is a dispute about damage, cleaning, missing items or deposit deductions at the end of the tenancy.
Residential.high: An inventory is important because it creates an agreed evidence record of the property's condition and contents at the start of the tenancy. A good inventory should describe rooms, fixtures, fittings, furnishings, appliances, cleanliness, decorative condition, defects, meter readings and keys — it should include photographs and be checked and agreed with the tenant. At the end of the tenancy, the check-out report can be compared against the inventory to identify deterioration beyond fair wear and tear. This protects both landlord and tenant — it helps landlords justify legitimate deposit deductions, while preventing unfair claims against tenants. Without a clear inventory, it may be very difficult to prove damage or loss in a deposit dispute.
Residential.referral: An inventory lists what is in the property.
referralWhy: Too basic — does not explain condition, evidence or deposit protection
challenge: What should be included in an inventory?

keyPoints: Inventories are evidence documents
Condition is as important as contents
They help prevent and resolve disputes
A poor inventory weakens deposit claims

Residential.q: How would you manage repairs in a residential let property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because repair management is a key part of residential property management and tenant care. They want to see whether candidates understand urgency, responsibility, communication and record keeping.
Residential.pass: I would log the repair request, identify the issue, assess urgency, check responsibility, obtain landlord approval where required and instruct an appropriate contractor. I would keep the tenant informed and record the action taken.
Residential.high: I would manage repairs through a structured process. First, I would record the tenant's report and gather enough information to understand the issue, including photographs where appropriate. I would assess urgency, especially where there is risk to health, safety, security, water ingress, heating, electrical safety or further property damage. I would then check responsibility under the tenancy agreement and relevant landlord obligations — if the landlord is responsible, I would obtain approval where required and instruct a competent contractor, and for emergencies action may need to be taken quickly to protect the tenant and property. I would keep the tenant and landlord informed, track completion, review invoices and retain records. Where repair issues were recurring, I would consider whether there was an underlying defect requiring further investigation rather than repeated temporary repair.
Residential.referral: I would ask a contractor to fix the problem.
referralWhy: Too basic — does not explain diagnosis, responsibility or urgency
challenge: How would you prioritise repairs?
What is an emergency repair?
What if the landlord refuses to repair?
How would you manage recurring defects?
keyPoints: Repair management requires urgency assessment
Communication and records are essential
Responsibility should be checked
Recurring problems may need deeper investigation

Residential.q: How would you deal with rent arrears in a residential tenancy?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because rent arrears affect landlord income and can quickly become sensitive. They want to see whether candidates can manage arrears professionally, lawfully and proportionately.
Residential.pass: I would contact the tenant promptly, confirm the arrears amount, check whether there is an explanation and ask for payment. I would keep records, update the landlord and consider a payment plan or formal action if arrears continued.
Residential.high: I would manage rent arrears promptly, professionally and in line with the tenancy agreement, landlord instructions and legal requirements. First, I would check the rent account to confirm the arrears and ensure there has been no banking or administration error. I would then contact the tenant in writing and, where appropriate, by phone to understand the reason for non-payment. If the arrears were short-term or caused by temporary difficulty, I may discuss a realistic payment plan, subject to landlord approval — I would keep the landlord updated and provide clear advice on the options and risks. If arrears continued, I would follow the appropriate escalation process, which may include formal notices or legal action through the landlord's solicitor. Throughout, I would keep accurate records of payments, communications, promises made and actions taken. The approach should be firm but fair, and should avoid harassment or unlawful pressure.

Legal escalation should follow proper process

Residential.q: What legal and regulatory issues should residential surveyors be aware of?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential work carries significant legal, regulatory and consumer protection responsibilities. They want to know whether candidates can identify key compliance areas and recognise when legal or specialist advice is required.
Residential.pass: Residential surveyors should be aware of issues such as consumer protection, estate agency obligations, leasehold matters, health and safety, planning, building regulations, energy performance, landlord and tenant requirements, anti-money laundering and data protection. They should also recognise when legal advice is needed.
Residential.high: Residential surveyors should understand the main legal and regulatory issues that affect valuation, agency, lettings, surveys and property management. These may include consumer protection requirements, estate agency duties, anti-money laundering, data protection, health and safety, energy performance, planning, building regulations, landlord and tenant obligations, leasehold information, deposit protection, safety certification, fire safety in flats and material information in marketing. In practice, I would ensure that my advice is accurate, clear and within my competence — for example, I may identify that a lease term, planning issue, building regulation matter or safety concern could affect value or marketability, but I would recommend solicitor or specialist advice where detailed legal interpretation is required. The key is to protect the client by identifying risk early, explaining its possible impact and ensuring the right professional advice is obtained before commitment.

Failing to link compliance to client risk

Residential.q: What is material information in residential property marketing?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential agents and advisers must ensure buyers and tenants are not misled. Material information is information that could affect a consumer's transactional decision.
Residential.pass: Material information is information that a buyer or tenant needs in order to make an informed decision about a property. It may include price, tenure, lease length, ground rent, service charge, council tax, EPC rating, parking, restrictions, defects, flood risk, planning issues or other matters that could affect their decision.
Residential.high: Material information is information that would be likely to influence a buyer or tenant's decision about whether to view, offer, rent or proceed with a property. In residential marketing, it is not enough to avoid false statements — important information should not be omitted where omission could mislead the consumer. Examples may include tenure, lease length, ground rent, service charge, council tax band, EPC rating, parking arrangements, access rights, restrictions, major works, known defects, planning matters, cladding or fire safety issues in flats, flood risk or unusual construction. As a residential professional, I would ensure property particulars are accurate, fair and not misleading — if I became aware of material information after marketing began, I would update the marketing and notify relevant parties where appropriate. The key is that consumers should be able to make informed decisions at the right stage of the transaction.

Residential.q: How would you manage anti-money laundering risk in residential agency?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential property can be used to launder money, and agents have duties to carry out proper checks. They want to know whether candidates understand AML as a real compliance risk, not a box-ticking exercise.
Residential.pass: I would follow my firm's anti-money laundering procedures, including verifying identity, understanding the client, checking source of funds where required, identifying beneficial owners and reporting suspicious activity internally. I would keep records and escalate concerns to the appropriate person.
Residential.high: I would manage anti-money laundering risk by following the firm's AML policy and applying a risk-based approach. This would include customer due diligence, verifying the identity of clients and relevant parties, understanding ownership structure, identifying beneficial owners where applicable, considering politically exposed persons or higher-risk jurisdictions, and understanding source of funds or source of wealth where required. I would remain alert to red flags, such as reluctance to provide information, unusual payment arrangements, unexplained third-party funds, complex ownership structures, pressure to move quickly without explanation or transactions that do not make commercial sense. If I had concerns, I would not ignore them or warn the client — I would escalate internally to the firm's nominated AML officer or follow the firm's suspicious activity reporting procedure.

Residential.q: How would you advise on Energy Performance Certificates in residential property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because energy performance affects compliance, running costs, letting, marketability and client advice. They want candidates to understand EPC relevance without overstepping into specialist energy assessment unless competent.
Residential.pass: An Energy Performance Certificate rates a property's energy efficiency and provides recommendations for improvement. It is relevant because it is usually required when a property is marketed for sale or let, and poor energy performance can affect running costs, marketability and letting compliance.
Residential.high: An EPC provides an energy efficiency rating and recommendations for improving performance. In residential advice, I would consider EPC rating because it can affect buyer or tenant perception, running costs, sustainability objectives and, in lettings, compliance with minimum energy efficiency requirements. For a seller or landlord, I would advise that an EPC should be available when required and that poor energy performance may affect marketability — for a buyer, I would explain that a low rating may indicate higher running costs or future improvement requirements. I would not provide specialist energy assessment unless qualified to do so, but I would consider the EPC as part of wider advice on value, lettability, compliance and future risk. Where the EPC rating is low, I may advise the client to consider improvement works, cost, practicality and whether specialist advice is needed.

Residential.q: How would you advise on fire safety issues in residential flats?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because fire safety in residential blocks can materially affect safety, value, mortgageability, service charges and saleability. They want candidates to recognise risk and recommend appropriate specialist advice.
Residential.pass: I would consider visible fire safety matters such as alarms, fire doors, escape routes, signage, communal areas, cladding, compartmentation concerns and management arrangements. If concerns were identified, I would recommend specialist fire safety advice and legal review of relevant documentation.
Residential.high: When advising on residential flats, I would consider fire safety as a material risk area, particularly in blocks with communal areas, external wall systems, cladding, complex layouts or known management issues. During inspection I may observe visible indicators such as fire doors, escape routes, communal fire safety arrangements, signage, alarms, emergency lighting, compartmentation concerns, external wall materials or blocked means of escape — however I would recognise the limits of a standard residential inspection. From a client advice perspective, fire safety issues can affect mortgageability, insurance, service charges, major works liability and buyer confidence. If concerns existed, I would recommend specialist fire safety advice, review of management information, fire risk assessments, external wall information where relevant and solicitor advice before exchange. I would avoid giving technical fire engineering advice unless competent and instructed to do so.

Residential.q: How would you advise on planning and building regulation issues in residential property?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because alterations, extensions and conversions are common in residential property. They want to see whether candidates can identify potential issues and advise further investigation without giving legal advice.
Residential.pass: I would look for signs of alterations, extensions, conversions or change of use and consider whether planning permission or building regulation approval may have been required. I would advise the client to ask their solicitor to check relevant approvals and completion certificates.
Residential.high: I would consider planning and building regulation issues where the property has been altered, extended, converted or used in a way that may require consent. During inspection I would look for evidence of extensions, loft conversions, garage conversions, structural alterations, removed walls, new windows, outbuildings, change of use, listed building or conservation area issues. Planning permission relates to whether development is permitted in planning terms, while building regulations relate to technical standards such as structure, fire safety, insulation, ventilation and drainage. I would not provide legal confirmation of compliance, but I would flag potential issues and recommend that the client's solicitor obtains planning permissions, building regulation approvals, completion certificates, lawful development certificates or indemnity advice where appropriate. The risk is that lack of approval may affect value, mortgageability, insurance, future saleability or require remedial works.

Residential.q: How would you manage data protection in residential practice?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential work involves personal data from clients, buyers, tenants, landlords and applicants. They want candidates to understand confidentiality, lawful handling and secure records.
Residential.pass: I would manage data protection by collecting only necessary personal data, using it for legitimate purposes, storing it securely, sharing it only where appropriate and following my firm's data protection policies. I would also be careful with emails, records and client information.
Residential.high: In residential practice, I would manage data protection by following my firm's policies and ensuring personal data is handled lawfully, securely and proportionately. Residential work may involve sensitive information such as identity documents, financial details, offers, tenancy applications, references, contact details and personal circumstances. I would collect only data needed for the instruction, explain how it will be used where required, store it securely, restrict access, avoid unnecessary disclosure and retain it only for the required period. I would also take care when sending emails, sharing documents, discussing offers or handling tenant referencing information. If there was a data breach or suspected breach, I would follow my firm's reporting procedure promptly.

Residential.q: How would you deal with a complaint from a residential client?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because complaints can arise in surveys, valuation, agency, lettings and management. They want to see whether candidates can respond professionally, calmly and in line with procedure.
Residential.pass: I would acknowledge the complaint, follow my firm's complaints handling procedure, record the details, investigate the issue, respond within required timescales and escalate where appropriate. I would remain professional and keep records of all communication.
Residential.high: If a residential client made a complaint, I would deal with it promptly, professionally and in accordance with my firm's complaints handling procedure. First, I would acknowledge the complaint and ensure it is recorded. I would clarify the nature of the complaint, review the file, correspondence, advice given, inspection notes, marketing records or tenancy records as relevant. I would avoid becoming defensive and would not admit liability without following the correct process — I would ensure the complaint is investigated by the appropriate person and responded to within the required timescale. If the complaint could not be resolved internally, I would explain the next stage of the process, including referral to the approved redress or dispute resolution route where applicable. Complaints should also be used as learning opportunities — if the issue arose from poor communication, unclear scope or process failure, I would consider what should be improved.

Complaints can highlight improvements

Residential.q: How would you avoid conflicts of interest in residential practice?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential professionals may act for sellers, buyers, landlords, tenants or lenders, and conflicts can arise easily. They want to know whether candidates understand actual, potential and perceived conflicts.
Residential.pass: I would check for conflicts before accepting an instruction. Conflicts may arise where the firm has acted for another party, has a financial interest, holds confidential information, or where personal relationships could affect objectivity. If a conflict exists, I would follow firm procedures and decide whether it can be managed or whether the instruction should be declined.
Residential.high: I would avoid conflicts of interest by checking for actual, potential and perceived conflicts before accepting or continuing an instruction. In residential practice, conflicts might arise where an agent is asked to advise both buyer and seller, where a surveyor has a personal interest in the property, where the firm holds confidential information from another client, or where a landlord and tenant both seek advice on the same matter. The issue is not only whether I believe I can act objectively, but whether a reasonable person would consider my independence or judgement compromised. If a conflict was identified, I would follow my firm's procedure, disclose the issue where appropriate, consider whether informed consent and safeguards could manage it, and decline the instruction if objectivity could not be protected. I would also keep clear records of conflict checks and decisions.

Residential.q: How would you protect vulnerable residential clients or consumers?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential professionals often deal with members of the public at stressful points: buying, selling, renting, bereavement, divorce, debt, relocation or health-related moves. They want candidates to understand professional care, communication and fairness.
Residential.pass: I would protect vulnerable clients by recognising signs of vulnerability, communicating clearly, allowing time for decisions, avoiding pressure, keeping records and involving appropriate support where needed. I would follow my firm's policies and treat the client fairly.
Residential.high: I would protect vulnerable clients or consumers by recognising that vulnerability may be temporary, situational or not immediately visible. Examples may include bereavement, illness, disability, financial pressure, language barriers, age-related difficulties, mental health challenges, domestic circumstances or unfamiliarity with property transactions. As a residential professional, I would adapt my communication, avoid jargon, confirm understanding, allow time for decisions, avoid pressure and ensure key advice is provided in writing. I would also be alert to undue influence or situations where a person may not fully understand the transaction — where appropriate, I may suggest the client involves a trusted adviser, family member, solicitor or support person, while respecting confidentiality and consent. The aim is not to make assumptions about someone's capacity, but to ensure they are treated fairly, respectfully and with appropriate care.

Residential.q: What was your personal role in the instruction?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because candidates often describe what the team or firm did rather than what they personally contributed. They need to assess the candidate's own competence.
Residential.pass: My personal role was to assist with the inspection, review property information, research comparable evidence and help prepare the advice to the client. I also helped identify key risks and ensured these were recorded in the report or client communication.
Residential.high: My personal role was to manage specific responsibilities, including inspection, evidence review, risk assessment, client communication and preparing part of the advice. For example, I inspected the property and identified a specific issue, such as a leasehold concern, damp risk, cracking, non-standard construction, short lease, service charge issue or weak comparable evidence. I then considered how that issue affected the client's decision — I reviewed the available evidence, discussed the issue with my supervisor or relevant specialist where appropriate, and helped formulate the advice. The key judgement I made was recommending further investigation before exchange, adjusting the valuation to reflect condition, advising against an unsupported asking price, or explaining that legal advice was required on a leasehold issue. Where I worked under supervision, I understood the reasoning behind the final advice and can explain how my contribution informed the client's decision.
Residential.referral: We inspected the property and advised the client on the best course of action.
referralWhy: Hides personal involvement — does not show what the candidate did or advised
Claiming responsibility they did not have
challenge: What did you personally inspect?
What advice came from you?
What judgement did you apply?
What would you do differently next time?
keyPoints: Personal role must be specific and honest
Supervised work can still demonstrate competence
Assessors want to understand your judgement
Avoid hiding behind the team
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: Why was your advice appropriate?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this to test whether the candidate can justify their advice. A strong answer explains how the advice was based on evidence, risk, client objectives and professional judgement.
Residential.pass: My advice was appropriate because it was based on the inspection findings, property information, comparable evidence and the client's objectives. I explained the main risks and recommended further advice where needed.
Residential.high: My advice was appropriate because it reflected the client's objective, the property evidence, the market position and the risks identified. For example, if the issue was valuation, I used relevant comparable evidence and adjusted it for differences in condition, location, size, tenure and marketability. If the issue was a defect, I explained the likely implications for repair cost, value, mortgageability or further investigation rather than giving a premature diagnosis. If the issue was leasehold, I flagged the impact on value and marketability but recommended solicitor or specialist advice where legal interpretation was required. The advice was therefore balanced — it did not simply tell the client what they wanted to hear, it helped them understand the risk and make an informed decision.
Residential.referral: My advice was appropriate because the client followed it.
referralWhy: Client acceptance does not prove advice was appropriate
challenge: What evidence supported your advice?
What alternatives did you consider?
Did you recommend further investigation?
How did the client use your advice?
keyPoints: Appropriate advice is evidence-based
Advice must reflect the client's objective
Risk and limitations should be explained
Good advice protects the client, not just the transaction
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: What was the greatest residential risk in your instruction?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this to see whether the candidate can identify a specific risk and explain its impact. Residential risks are often practical, emotional and financial because clients may be making major personal decisions.
Residential.pass: The greatest risk was a specific issue, such as a defect, short lease, poor market evidence, service charge uncertainty, mortgageability issue or compliance concern. I managed this by identifying the risk, explaining the potential impact to the client and recommending further investigation or specialist advice where required.
Residential.high: The greatest residential risk could have affected the client's decision, value, mortgageability, repair liability or future saleability. For example, if the risk was suspected structural movement, I explained that the issue could affect value, insurance and lender confidence, and recommended structural engineer advice before the client proceeded. If the risk was leasehold, such as a short lease or uncertain service charge liability, I explained that it could affect marketability and affordability, and advised the client to obtain solicitor and specialist advice before exchange. If the risk was weak market evidence, I explained the valuation uncertainty and how much reliance could reasonably be placed on the figure. I managed the risk by being specific, proportionate and clear about what the client should do next.
Residential.referral: The biggest risk was that the client might make the wrong decision.
referralWhy: Too general — does not identify the actual property, market, legal or compliance risk
challenge: Why was that the greatest risk?
How did it affect value or marketability?
What further advice did you recommend?
What was the residual risk?
keyPoints: Strong risk answers are specific
Risk should be linked to client decision-making
Further investigation should be proportionate
The client must understand impact and next steps
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: How did you manage client expectations?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential clients may have strong emotional and financial expectations. Candidates must show that they can communicate difficult advice clearly and professionally.
Residential.pass: I managed expectations by explaining the scope of my advice, the evidence available, the risks identified and any limitations. Where the client had unrealistic expectations, I explained the position using evidence and kept records of the advice given.
Residential.high: I managed client expectations by giving clear, evidence-based advice, especially where the client's expectations did not align with the evidence. For example, if a seller expected a higher asking price than the market supported, I explained the comparable evidence, current competing stock and the risk of overpricing, such as reduced interest, longer marketing period and later price reduction. If a buyer underestimated the seriousness of a defect, I explained the potential implications for repair cost, mortgageability and future saleability, and recommended further investigation before commitment. I also clarified the scope and limitations of my role — for example, I could advise on valuation and marketability impact, but legal lease interpretation or specialist structural diagnosis required appropriate professional input. Managing expectations is important because residential clients often make emotional decisions, and my role is to provide calm, objective advice that helps them make informed choices.
Residential.referral: I tried to explain everything clearly so the client understood.
referralWhy: Good intention but lacks a specific example or professional judgement
Telling the client what they want to hear
challenge: What if the client disagreed with your advice?
How would you explain bad news?
How would you avoid overstepping your role?
Why is written advice important?
keyPoints: Residential clients may need careful expectation management
Evidence helps difficult conversations
Scope and limitations should be clear
Good advice may not always be what the client wants to hear
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: How did you protect your client's interests?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this to test whether the candidate understands client care as professional protection, not simply being helpful. In residential work, protecting the client often means identifying risk before they commit.
Residential.pass: I protected the client by identifying key risks, explaining their potential impact and recommending appropriate next steps. I also ensured my advice was clear, accurate, within my competence and recorded properly.
Residential.high: I protected my client's interests by ensuring they understood the key risks before making a decision. For example, if advising a purchaser, I identified matters that could affect value, mortgageability, repair liability or future saleability, and where necessary recommended further investigation before exchange. If advising a seller, I provided realistic market advice and explained the risks of overpricing, poor presentation or failing to disclose material information. If advising a landlord or tenant, I considered compliance, affordability, property condition, safety obligations and documentation. I also protected the client by staying within my competence — where legal, structural, fire safety, asbestos, leasehold or specialist advice was required, I flagged the issue and advised the client to seek the appropriate professional input. Client protection is not simply completing the transaction — it is ensuring the client understands the consequences of proceeding.
Residential.referral: I protected the client by giving them the best advice I could.
referralWhy: Too vague — does not explain what risk was managed or how
Prioritising transaction completion over client protection
challenge: What specific risk did you protect against?
Did you recommend further investigation?
How did you avoid acting outside competence?
How did you record your advice?
keyPoints: Client protection means clear risk advice
Residential advice should support informed decisions
Competence limits must be respected
Records protect both client and surveyor
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: How did you deal with limited or imperfect information?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this because residential instructions often involve incomplete information, inaccessible areas, missing documents or uncertain evidence. They want to see whether the candidate can manage uncertainty professionally.
Residential.pass: Where information was missing, I identified the gap, considered whether it affected my advice and recorded any assumptions or limitations. If the missing information was material, I recommended further enquiries or specialist advice.
Residential.high: I dealt with limited information by first assessing whether the missing information was material to the client's decision. For example, if I could not access a loft, I would record the limitation and consider whether roof defects, insulation, ventilation or structural alterations could still be material. If lease documents were unavailable, I would not assume the lease terms were acceptable — I would flag the issue for solicitor review. In valuation, if comparable evidence was limited, I would widen the search carefully, consider weaker evidence with caution and explain any valuation uncertainty. The key was to avoid false certainty — I would make only reasonable assumptions, state them clearly and advise further investigation where the issue could affect value, marketability, safety or mortgageability.
Residential.referral: I made assumptions where information was missing.
referralWhy: Does not explain whether assumptions were reasonable, recorded or communicated
challenge: What information was missing?
How did it affect your advice?
How did you report limitations?
When would missing information prevent you from advising?
keyPoints: Missing information should be assessed for materiality
Assumptions must be reasonable and recorded
Limitations should be explained clearly
Clients should understand uncertainty
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: What would you do differently if undertaking the instruction again?
Residential.why: Assessors ask this to test reflection and professional maturity. They are not expecting perfection — they want candidates to show what they learned and how they improved.
Residential.pass: If undertaking the instruction again, I would gather more information earlier, clarify the client's objectives more fully or record limitations more clearly. This would have improved the advice process and reduced uncertainty.
Residential.high: If undertaking the instruction again, I would improve a specific area, because it would have reduced risk or strengthened the advice. For example, I may have requested leasehold information earlier, asked more detailed questions about the client's intended use, obtained more comparable evidence, recorded inspection limitations more clearly, or recommended specialist advice sooner. The key learning was that residential advice often depends on identifying material risks early, especially before exchange, marketing or tenancy commitment. I have since applied this learning by using a more structured inspection checklist, improving client briefing questions, recording assumptions more clearly or flagging further investigation needs earlier. This shows that I reflected on the instruction and improved my future practice.
Residential.referral: I would not do anything differently because the instruction went well.
referralWhy: Shows limited reflection — even successful instructions provide learning points
challenge: What was your main learning point?
Did anything go wrong?
How have you changed your approach since?
What feedback did you receive?
keyPoints: Reflection shows professionalism
Improvements should be specific
Learning should affect future practice
Strong candidates can reflect without sounding incompetent
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: Why do Residential pathway candidates get referred?
Residential.why: Assessors may ask this to test whether the candidate understands the assessment standard. They want to see whether the candidate knows the difference between describing residential work and demonstrating professional competence.
Residential.pass: Residential candidates may get referred if they cannot explain valuation evidence, inspection findings, leasehold risks, client advice, regulatory issues or their personal role. They may also struggle if they give generic answers or act outside their competence.
Residential.high: Residential candidates often get referred because they describe what happened but do not explain their professional judgement. Common weaknesses include weak valuation evidence, poor explanation of comparable adjustments, superficial defect advice, limited leasehold understanding, failure to explain client risk, overuse of 'we', and giving legal or specialist advice beyond competence. Candidates may also be referred if they cannot explain how their advice protected the client — in residential work this is critical because clients are often making high-value, personal and emotionally charged decisions. At Level 3, assessors expect candidates to explain the issue, evidence, risk, advice, outcome and reflection. A strong answer should show that the candidate can identify material residential risk and give clear, proportionate client advice.
Residential.referral: Residential candidates get referred because they do not know enough about property defects or valuation.
referralWhy: Technical knowledge matters but many referrals arise from weak demonstration of judgement
challenge: What makes a Residential answer weak?
How do you demonstrate Level 3 judgement?
Why is client care so important in residential work?
What residential risks commonly affect value?
keyPoints: Referral often comes from weak demonstration, not lack of experience
Residential candidates must show judgement and client care
Personal involvement must be clear
Level 3 answers need evidence, risk, advice and outcome
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: Why should RICS award you MRICS status?
Residential.why: This is a final professionalism question. Assessors want to know whether the candidate understands that chartered status is a responsibility, not simply a reward for completing the APC.
Residential.pass: RICS should award me MRICS status because I have developed the required residential property knowledge and practical experience. I understand the importance of acting professionally, advising clients clearly, managing risk and working within my competence.
Residential.high: RICS should award me MRICS status because I have demonstrated the technical competence, professional judgement and ethical awareness expected of a Chartered Surveyor. Through my Residential pathway experience, I understand that clients rely on surveyors at important and often stressful points in their lives, including buying, selling, renting, managing or investing in property. I recognise that my advice must be objective, evidence-based, clear and within my competence — where I identify issues such as defects, leasehold risk, valuation uncertainty, compliance concerns or specialist matters, I must explain the implications and recommend appropriate next steps. Being chartered is not simply about completing the APC — it means acting with integrity, maintaining competence, protecting clients, treating consumers fairly and upholding public confidence in the profession. I believe I am ready because I can combine residential technical knowledge with client care, risk awareness, communication skills and professional judgement.
Residential.referral: Because I have completed my APC, worked hard and gained experience in residential property.
referralWhy: Does not demonstrate professional readiness, ethics or responsibility
Not mentioning ethics or public trust
challenge: What does being chartered mean to you?
How will you maintain competence?
What would you do if asked to act outside your competence?
How do residential surveyors protect the public?
keyPoints: MRICS status is a professional responsibility
Residential clients rely heavily on surveyor advice
Chartered Surveyors must act ethically and objectively
Strong candidates show readiness, judgement and public trust
Residential.module: Case Study, Client Advice & Final Assessment

Residential.q: What fraud risks should you be aware of in residential loan security valuation, and what should you do if you identify concerns?
Residential.why: Loan security valuation L1 requires fraud and criminal activity awareness; L2 requires the ability to identify and report fraud to the National Crime Agency or equivalent. Residential mortgage fraud is a known risk area and assessors expect candidates selecting this competency to understand both the types of fraud encountered and the correct reporting obligations.
Residential.pass: I would be aware that residential loan security valuation can be subject to fraud, including inflated valuations, identity fraud, misrepresented property characteristics or fabricated transactions. If I identified concerns, I would not proceed without raising the matter internally with my supervisor and following my firm's reporting procedures.
Residential.high: Loan security valuation fraud can take various forms. Common examples include inflated valuations to support a larger mortgage loan, misrepresentation of the property's condition, specification, tenure or identity, back-to-back or same-day transactions at prices above market value, straw buyer arrangements where the true purchaser is concealed, and fabricated rental income to support buy-to-let lending decisions. During a valuation I would be alert to red flags such as an agreed price significantly above comparable evidence, pressure from any party to reach a specific figure, an unusually urgent instruction without clear commercial explanation, inconsistencies in property documentation or ownership, or a transaction that does not make commercial sense. If I identified or suspected fraud, I would first escalate internally to my supervisor or the firm's money laundering reporting officer — I would not alert the client or any suspected party, as doing so could constitute tipping off. Where required, the firm's nominated officer may need to submit a suspicious activity report to the National Crime Agency or equivalent authority. Throughout, my valuation opinion would remain independent of any commercial or client pressure to adjust the figure.
Residential.referral: I would tell my manager if I thought something was wrong.
referralWhy: No awareness of specific fraud types in loan security valuation
Fails to mention the NCA reporting obligation required at L2
Does not identify the tipping-off risk or internal escalation process
Does not demonstrate that valuation opinion must remain independent under pressure
challenge: What types of fraud are most commonly encountered in residential mortgage valuation?
What would you do if a broker or client pressured you to adjust your valuation figure upwards?
What is the difference between reporting internally to your MLRO and submitting a SAR to the NCA?
What is tipping off and why does it matter in this context?
keyPoints: Loan security valuation L1 requires fraud and criminal activity awareness
Loan security valuation L2 requires reporting fraud to the National Crime Agency or equivalent
Internal escalation to the firm's MLRO comes first — never alert the suspected party
Valuation opinion must remain independent regardless of commercial or client pressure

Residential.q: How does sustainability apply to residential property practice, and what is Triple Bottom Line analysis?
Residential.why: Sustainability L1 requires knowledge of the legal and policy framework and the relationship between property and sustainability. Sustainability L2 requires the ability to apply Triple Bottom Line analysis to residential scenarios — TBL is the specific sustainability framework named by the RICS Residential pathway guide for this competency at L2.
Residential.pass: Sustainability in residential property relates to energy performance, environmental impact, social wellbeing and long-term economic viability. Triple Bottom Line analysis considers three dimensions — economic, social and environmental — to give a rounded assessment of sustainability. In practice this might include considering running costs and energy bills, occupant and community wellbeing, and carbon and environmental impact.
Residential.high: The Brundtland Commission defined sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. In residential property, sustainability encompasses energy performance, carbon impact, resource use, community and social impact, and long-term economic viability. Triple Bottom Line analysis applies three dimensions: economic — covering running costs, energy bills, asset value, lettability and investment return; social — covering occupant health and wellbeing, community benefit, affordability and accessibility; and environmental — covering carbon emissions, energy efficiency, biodiversity, water use and materials. In a residential instruction, I would consider sustainability when advising on energy performance, refurbishment options, lettings compliance, and asset management. For lettings, the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards require domestic let properties to meet a minimum EPC rating — advising a landlord on compliance, improvement options and cost is a direct sustainability task. At an advisory level, I would apply TBL analysis to evaluate residential decisions in a rounded way, not solely on financial return, and advise on how sustainability improvements affect value, marketability, regulatory risk and long-term running costs.
Residential.referral: Sustainability means making properties more energy efficient.
referralWhy: Reduces sustainability to EPC alone — no awareness of TBL or the broader framework
No reference to Triple Bottom Line or its three economic, social and environmental dimensions
Fails to connect sustainability to professional advice, value impact or regulatory compliance
challenge: What is the Brundtland definition of sustainable development?
How would you apply Triple Bottom Line analysis to a specific residential instruction?
What are the minimum energy efficiency requirements for residential let properties?
How would you advise a landlord whose property has a low EPC rating?
keyPoints: Triple Bottom Line = economic, social and environmental sustainability dimensions
Sustainability L2 requires TBL analysis applied to residential scenarios — it is specifically named in the RICS Residential pathway guide
MEES requires domestic let properties to meet a minimum EPC rating before lawful letting
Sustainability affects value, lettability, running costs, compliance and professional advice

Residential.q: What dispute resolution procedures are available for residential property disputes, and when would you recommend each?
Residential.why: Conflict avoidance L1 requires knowledge of specific dispute resolution procedures including PACT, the RICS Dispute Resolution Service, the Valuation Tribunal and litigation. L2 requires understanding of how these apply in practice, including Regulation 17 of the Alteration of Lists and Appeals Regulations in the context of Council Tax band appeals. Assessors expect candidates selecting this optional competency to name and distinguish the specific procedures.
Residential.pass: Dispute resolution options include negotiation, mediation, independent expert determination, arbitration, PACT, the RICS Dispute Resolution Service, the Valuation Tribunal and litigation. I would recommend the least adversarial route first and escalate only where resolution cannot be reached, advising clients on the cost, speed, binding nature and formality of each option.
Residential.high: The main dispute resolution procedures available for residential property disputes range from informal to highly formal. Negotiation should always be the first approach — it is the least costly and preserves relationships. Where negotiation fails, mediation involves a neutral third party facilitating agreement, without imposing a decision. Independent expert determination provides a binding decision by a specialist appointed by agreement, often used for technical disputes such as valuations or boundary matters. Arbitration is a formal binding procedure governed by the Arbitration Act 1996. PACT — Professional Arbitration on Court Terms — is a specific procedure used for rent review and residential leasehold disputes, providing a faster and less costly route than litigation where parties accept the arbitration framework. The RICS Dispute Resolution Service provides specialist adjudication, expert determination and mediation services administered by RICS for disputes in the built environment, including those involving RICS-regulated professionals. The Valuation Tribunal handles Council Tax banding and non-domestic rating appeals — in a residential context, Regulation 17 of the Alteration of Lists and Appeals Regulations governs how a Council Tax band can be challenged and the process for applying to alter the valuation list. Calderbank offers and Part 36 offers can be used strategically in proceedings to protect a party's costs position if the matter goes to a formal hearing. My advice to a client would consider the nature and value of the dispute, the relationship between parties, speed and cost, and whether a binding outcome is needed — I would recommend the least adversarial route capable of achieving a fair resolution before recommending formal or adversarial proceedings.
Residential.referral: I would recommend the client go to court.
referralWhy: Litigation is the most adversarial and expensive route — recommending it immediately shows no awareness of alternatives
No mention of PACT, RICS Dispute Resolution Service, Valuation Tribunal or Regulation 17
Fails to demonstrate any knowledge of the conflict avoidance principle or the spectrum of dispute resolution options
challenge: When would you recommend PACT over independent expert determination?
What is the RICS Dispute Resolution Service and in what circumstances is it used?
What is Regulation 17 and when does it apply in a residential context?
What is the difference between a Calderbank offer and a Part 36 offer, and why does it matter in dispute proceedings?
keyPoints: PACT is used for rent review and residential leasehold disputes — a faster and less costly alternative to litigation
RICS Dispute Resolution Service provides RICS-administered adjudication, expert determination and mediation
Valuation Tribunal handles Council Tax band appeals — Regulation 17 of the Alteration of Lists and Appeals Regulations governs how the list can be altered
Always consider least adversarial options first — cost, speed, binding effect and relationship preservation all matter

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you advise a landlord on the appropriate quoting rent for a commercial property?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to see whether you can move beyond simply collecting comparable evidence and provide reasoned commercial advice about market evidence, property characteristics and client objectives.
