Commercial Real Estate.pass: When advising a landlord on quoting rent I would review recent comparable lettings considering location, size, specification, lease terms, incentives and condition. I would assess competing stock and tenant demand, then provide a recommended quoting rent supported by evidence.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would explain the risks of setting rent too high — reduced enquiries, extended void period and increased holding costs — and the risk of setting it too low and missing the opportunity to maximise rental income. My final advice would be linked to the landlord's objective. If they wanted a quick letting I may recommend a competitive quoting rent. If they were prepared to wait I may recommend testing the market at a higher level but reviewing feedback regularly.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would set the rent based on what the landlord wants.
referralWhy: No consideration of risk or client objectives
challenge: What makes a good comparable?
How would you adjust evidence from a different building?
How do incentives affect effective rent?
What would you do if the landlord insisted on an unrealistic quoting rent?
keyPoints: Assessors test reasoning not the rent figure
Analyse comparables and adjust for property factors
Link advice to client objectives
Explain risks of pricing too high or too low

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you advise a tenant considering a new office lease?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to see whether you understand that lease advice is about more than rent and can identify wider commercial risks and obligations affecting the tenant.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: When advising a tenant on a new office lease I would begin by understanding their business requirements including location, size, budget, occupational timescale and need for flexibility. I would then review the proposed heads of terms and identify the main commercial issues including rent, lease term, rent review, service charge, repairing obligations, break clauses and alienation provisions.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would advise the tenant not just on headline rent but on total occupational cost and long-term liability. A full repairing and insuring lease could create significant future dilapidations exposure so I would recommend the client considers limiting liability through a schedule of condition where appropriate. I would also consider whether the lease gives sufficient flexibility — if the client expected growth or uncertainty I would advise on break options, assignment and underletting rights.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would focus on getting the lowest possible rent.
referralWhy: Ignores service charge and repair liability
Fails to consider tenant's future plans
challenge: What is an FRI lease?
Why might a schedule of condition be useful?
What is the difference between assignment and underletting?
Why are break clauses often heavily negotiated?
keyPoints: Good tenant advice protects from future liability not just immediate cost
Consider total occupational cost
Advise on flexibility and future options
Explain repairing obligations clearly

Commercial Real Estate.q: What factors influence commercial rental value?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Rental value is central to leasing, valuation and landlord and tenant advice. Assessors want to see whether candidates understand value drivers and can explain them commercially.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Commercial rental value is influenced by property-specific factors including location, size, specification, condition, layout, accessibility, parking and energy performance. Market factors include supply and demand, tenant activity, competing stock and economic conditions.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Lease terms also influence rental value. A longer lease with strong tenant covenant may support a different rental tone compared with a shorter or more flexible lease. Incentives such as rent-free periods affect the effective rent achieved. When advising a client I would not simply list these factors — I would explain how each affects rental value in that particular market.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Rental value is mainly about location.
challenge: How does lease length affect rental value?
How do incentives affect rental evidence?
What is the difference between headline rent and effective rent?
How does EPC rating influence marketability?
keyPoints: Rental value is formed by interpreting property evidence within market context
Consider both property-specific and market factors
Lease terms and incentives affect effective rent
Never treat headline rent as achieved rent

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you conduct a commercial property viewing?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to see whether you understand agency practice, client care, presentation, compliance and risk management. A viewing is not simply opening the door — it is part of the leasing or sales process.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Before conducting a viewing I would ensure I understood the property, the client's instructions, the marketing details and key lease or sale terms. I would consider health and safety including access arrangements, hazards, lighting and whether PPE was required.
Commercial Real Estate.high: During the viewing I would explain key features including size, specification, services, access, amenities and lease terms. I would answer questions accurately and avoid giving unverified information. I would also use the viewing to understand the occupier's requirements including timing, budget and fit-out needs. After the viewing I would report feedback to the client and agree next steps.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would show them around and answer any questions.
challenge: What health and safety checks would you make before a viewing?
What should you do if you are unsure of the answer to a question?
How do you avoid misrepresentation?
What information would you report back to the landlord?
keyPoints: A viewing is part of the professional advice process
Prepare, control, verify and follow up
Never give unverified answers
Health and safety must be considered

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you advise a landlord regarding incentive packages?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Incentives are central to commercial leasing. Assessors want to see whether candidates understand the difference between headline rent and effective rent.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: I would advise a landlord that incentives are used to secure tenant commitment, particularly where there is competing supply or where tenants require support with fit-out costs. Common incentives include rent-free periods, stepped rents, capital contributions or landlord works.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would explain the difference between headline rent and effective rent. A landlord may achieve a strong headline rent but offer a long rent-free period which reduces the effective rent over the lease term. My advice would compare the proposed incentive package against market evidence and link it to the landlord's objective. A strong covenant tenant on a longer lease may justify a more attractive incentive package.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would offer whatever the tenant asks for to secure the letting.
referralWhy: Fails to consider market conditions or tenant covenant
challenge: What is a rent-free period?
How do you calculate effective rent?
Why might a landlord offer a capital contribution?
What if the tenant asks for an excessive incentive?
keyPoints: Incentives are a commercial tool assessed as part of the total package
Headline rent does not equal effective rent
Link incentive advice to market conditions and client objectives
Consider void costs when advising on incentives

Commercial Real Estate.q: What information should be included within marketing particulars?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to see whether candidates understand agency best practice, accurate marketing and the need to avoid misleading information.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Marketing particulars should include the property address, description, accommodation schedule, floor areas, tenure, rent or price, EPC rating, planning use, business rates, service charge where relevant, lease or sale terms, photographs, plans and viewing arrangements.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would ensure information is verified before publication — floor areas should be measured or confirmed and planning use and service charge information checked with the client or managing agent. I would include appropriate disclaimers but would not rely on them to justify inaccurate or misleading information.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would include whatever makes the property look good.
referralWhy: Treats particulars as sales material only
challenge: Why is accuracy important in marketing particulars?
What could happen if particulars are misleading?
How should floor areas be reported?
What would you do if information had not yet been confirmed?
keyPoints: Marketing particulars are professional documents not just promotional material
Accuracy is a professional obligation
Verify information before publishing
Disclaimers do not justify misleading information

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you manage multiple competing offers?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to test judgement, fairness, transparency and ability to advise the client when there is competitive interest.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: If multiple offers were received I would record each one clearly and ensure sufficient information was provided for comparison. I would analyse headline rent or price, tenant covenant, lease term, incentives requested, funding position, conditions attached and timing.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would present the offers to the client in a structured way explaining the strengths and risks of each. The highest offer may not always be the best if it carries greater uncertainty or a weaker covenant. Depending on the level of interest I may recommend a best and final offers process, ensuring it was handled transparently and fairly with clear deadlines.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would recommend the highest offer.
challenge: Is the highest offer always the best offer?
What is a best and final offers process?
How would you assess tenant covenant?
How would you document your advice?
keyPoints: A strong offer is about certainty and deliverability not just price
Assess covenant, conditions and timing alongside rent
Handle competing offers transparently and fairly
Document advice clearly

Commercial Real Estate.q: What are the risks associated with Heads of Terms?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to know whether you understand the importance and limitations of Heads of Terms in leasing and sale transactions.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Heads of Terms set out the agreed commercial terms of a proposed transaction. They are usually subject to contract and not generally intended to be legally binding. The main risk is that unclear or incomplete terms can cause delay, disagreement or legal uncertainty.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Important terms such as rent, lease length, break clauses, rent review, repairing obligations, service charge and incentives should all be clearly recorded. I would ensure Heads of Terms accurately reflect the negotiated position and advise the client to obtain legal advice before entering binding commitments. I would be careful not to stray into legal advice — my role is to agree and record the commercial terms.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Heads of Terms are just a formality before the lawyers take over.
referralWhy: Underestimates importance of Heads of Terms
Ignores risk of unclear or missing terms
challenge: Are Heads of Terms legally binding?
What does subject to contract mean?
What key terms should be included?
When should solicitors become involved?
keyPoints: Good Heads of Terms reduce transaction risk
Poor Heads of Terms create confusion delay and dispute
Record all commercial terms clearly
Do not stray into legal advice

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you advise a client regarding an Agreement for Lease?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to know whether candidates understand the commercial purpose and risk of Agreements for Lease which are common where a lease will be granted in the future.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: An Agreement for Lease is a legally binding agreement where parties commit to enter into a lease at a future date, usually once certain conditions have been satisfied. It may be used where the property is under construction, refurbishment works are required or planning consent is needed.
Commercial Real Estate.high: When advising a client I would explain the commercial purpose and key risks. For a landlord it can secure tenant commitment before works are completed. For a tenant it provides certainty over future occupation. The agreement must clearly set out conditions, timescales, specification of works, longstop dates, rent commencement and consequences if obligations are not met. I would recommend legal advice because the Agreement for Lease creates binding obligations.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: An Agreement for Lease is the same as Heads of Terms.
referralWhy: Confuses Agreement for Lease with Heads of Terms
Does not recognise it can be legally binding
Ignores importance of conditions and timescales
challenge: When might an Agreement for Lease be used?
What is a condition precedent?
What is a longstop date?
How does it differ from Heads of Terms?
keyPoints: An Agreement for Lease creates binding future obligations
Risk lies in unclear obligations conditions and timescales
Distinguish clearly from Heads of Terms
Always recommend legal advice

Commercial Real Estate.q: How do you demonstrate best practice during an agency instruction?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Agency work carries professional ethical and regulatory responsibilities. Assessors want to see that candidates understand how to act professionally, transparently and in the client's best interests.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Best practice starts with clear instructions from the client. I would ensure scope, fees, marketing strategy, reporting arrangements and basis of instruction were agreed in writing. Before accepting the instruction I would consider conflicts of interest.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Throughout the instruction I would ensure marketing information was accurate, enquiries handled professionally and all offers recorded and reported promptly to the client. I would maintain clear records of advice, negotiations and decisions — important for both client care and professional protection. I would also agree a marketing strategy including quoting terms, target occupiers, marketing channels and timescales.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would focus on getting the deal done as quickly as possible.
referralWhy: No mention of terms of engagement
challenge: What should be included in terms of engagement?
How would you identify a conflict of interest?
How should offers be reported?
Why is record keeping important?
keyPoints: Agency best practice starts before the transaction begins
Terms of engagement and conflict checks are essential
Record all advice negotiations and offers
Act professionally transparently and in the client's best interests

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is the purpose of a rent review?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors test whether you understand the commercial purpose of rent reviews and how they operate within a lease, not just a definition.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: A rent review is a lease mechanism that allows the rent to be reviewed at agreed intervals during the lease term. I would first review the lease carefully to understand the review mechanism, assumptions, disregards, review date and notice requirements. I would then gather and analyse comparable evidence considering location, size, specification, lease terms and incentives.
Commercial Real Estate.high: The rent review can have significant financial implications for both landlord and tenant so it is important that advice is properly evidenced and clearly communicated. I would not simply apply a general market view — my advice would be based on the specific lease terms and market evidence. I would also explain the difference between types of review including open market, indexed and fixed increases.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: A rent review means the rent will go up at the review date.
referralWhy: Confuses rent review with lease renewal
No mention of assumptions and disregards
challenge: What types of rent review are commonly used?
What are assumptions and disregards?
What happens if the parties cannot agree?
Why is lease wording so important?
keyPoints: Rent reviews are governed by the lease
The basis of review must be understood before giving advice
Evidence and interpretation are both important
Consider the commercial impact on the client

Commercial Real Estate.q: Explain the difference between upward-only and indexed rent reviews.
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to see whether you understand different rent review mechanisms and their commercial implications for landlord and tenant.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: An upward-only rent review means the rent can increase or remain the same at review but cannot decrease even if market rental values have fallen. An indexed rent review links rent increases to an index such as inflation, providing more certainty through a formula-based calculation.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Upward-only reviews protect landlord income but can leave tenants paying above-market rent during weaker conditions. Indexed reviews provide certainty but the lease must be reviewed carefully to understand the specific index, whether there is a cap and collar, and how the calculation is applied. Each mechanism has different risks and benefits — open market reviews rely on market evidence whereas indexed reviews follow a formula.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: All rent reviews are the same — they just increase the rent.
referralWhy: Assumes all reviews are open market
challenge: What is a cap and collar?
Why might a tenant prefer an indexed rent review?
Why might a landlord prefer upward-only reviews?
How would inflation affect indexed reviews?
keyPoints: Upward-only reviews protect landlord income
Indexed reviews provide formula-based certainty
Caps and collars can limit risk for either party
Rent review advice must always begin with the lease

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you prepare for a rent review negotiation?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to understand whether you can prepare a professional negotiation strategy based on evidence, lease interpretation and client objectives.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: I would begin by reviewing the lease to understand the rent review clause, review date, assumptions, disregards and dispute resolution provisions. I would then gather relevant comparable rental evidence and analyse each comparable carefully considering location, size, condition, specification, lease terms and incentives.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would form a justified opinion of rental value on the review basis set out in the lease and consider the strengths and weaknesses of both my client's position and the likely position of the other party. Before entering negotiations I would agree a strategy with my client including the preferred outcome, acceptable range and commercial factors that may influence settlement. I would keep records of discussions and advise on the risks and costs of proceeding to third-party determination if agreement could not be reached.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would tell the other party what rent I think is right and negotiate from there.
challenge: How would you select comparable evidence?
What if the other party relies on stronger evidence?
What is third-party determination?
How would you advise your client on settlement?
keyPoints: Preparation is evidence-led
The lease controls the review basis
Negotiation strategy should reflect both evidence and client objectives
Settlement can be preferable to costly dispute

Commercial Real Estate.q: What evidence would you rely upon during a rent review?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to test whether you understand what makes evidence reliable and how comparable evidence should be analysed.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: I would rely primarily on recent open market lettings of comparable properties where the evidence reflects the review basis set out in the lease. I would consider location, size, specification, condition, lease terms, incentives, tenant covenant and date of transaction.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would be careful to distinguish between headline rent and effective rent, particularly where incentives such as rent-free periods were granted. If evidence was limited I may also consider asking rents or wider market evidence but I would place less weight on these than completed comparable transactions. My advice would explain the quality of the evidence and any adjustments made.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would use the most recent letting I could find.
referralWhy: Uses asking rents as if completed evidence
challenge: What makes a comparable reliable?
How do incentives affect rental evidence?
Would you rely on asking rents?
What if there were no direct comparables?
keyPoints: Comparable evidence must be analysed not just collected
Completed lettings carry more weight than asking rents
Lease terms and incentives can materially affect evidence
Explain the strength and weakness of your evidence

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is interim rent?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Interim rent is a technical landlord and tenant topic that often appears in lease renewal discussions. Assessors use it to test whether you understand the financial implications of statutory lease renewal.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Interim rent is the rent payable during the period between the end of the contractual lease term and the commencement of the new lease, where the tenant remains in occupation under statutory protection. Under the Regulatory Reform (Business Tenancies) Order 2003, either party — landlord or tenant — may apply to the court for an interim rent determination; previously only the landlord could apply. Where the court grants a new tenancy on the same terms at the same holding, interim rent is presumed to match the rent under the new lease, unless it would be substantially different — for example due to a significant change in market conditions between the lease expiry and the new term commencing.
Commercial Real Estate.high: It commonly arises under the lease renewal process where parties have not yet completed the new lease. The level may be determined by agreement or by the court. The 2003 Order presumption — that interim rent equals the new lease rent in unopposed, like-for-like renewals — has real practical significance: a tenant who secures a new lease at a reduced rent may benefit from that lower figure applying back through the interim period, rather than continuing to pay a higher historic rent throughout. When advising a client I would explain that interim rent can have financial implications and should be considered as part of the wider lease renewal strategy. I would also recommend legal advice because the statutory process and timing can affect the position.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Interim rent is the same as the current passing rent.
referralWhy: Not linked to statutory lease renewal
challenge: When does interim rent arise?
Is interim rent always the same as the old passing rent?
How does lease renewal timing affect interim rent?
Who determines interim rent if not agreed?
keyPoints: Interim rent is linked to protected lease renewals
It covers the period between lease expiry and the new lease
It can have financial implications for both parties
Work with solicitors on the legal process

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you advise a landlord regarding lease renewal?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Lease renewal is a key area of Commercial Real Estate practice. Assessors want to see whether you can advise strategically not just explain the process.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: When advising a landlord on lease renewal I would first review the existing lease to establish expiry date, whether the tenant has security of tenure and key lease terms. I would then discuss the landlord's objectives — they may want to retain the tenant, improve the rent, vary terms, redevelop or regain possession.
Commercial Real Estate.high: If the tenant has statutory protection I would advise that the renewal process must be handled carefully and legal advice obtained regarding notices and statutory procedure. From a surveying perspective I would advise on market rent, proposed lease length, rent review provisions, repairing obligations and service charge. My recommendation would balance income, risk, future asset strategy and the landlord's wider objectives.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would tell the landlord what rent they can get and handle the renewal.
challenge: What is security of tenure?
What notices may be served in a lease renewal?
Why might a landlord oppose renewal?
What if the landlord wants to redevelop?
keyPoints: Lease renewal advice is strategic not just procedural
Security of tenure is a key starting point
The landlord's objectives shape the advice
Rent risk timing and future plans all matter

Commercial Real Estate.q: What rights arise under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954?
Commercial Real Estate.why: The Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 is central to commercial lease renewals in England and Wales. Assessors want to check that candidates understand security of tenure and its practical implications.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: The Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 provides security of tenure for qualifying business tenants unless the lease has been validly contracted out. A protected tenant may have the right to remain in occupation and request a new lease on terms to be agreed or determined.
Commercial Real Estate.high: A landlord cannot simply require the tenant to leave unless statutory grounds for opposition apply — such as redevelopment, own occupation, persistent delay in paying rent or breach of repairing obligations. When advising a client I would first establish whether the lease is protected or contracted out and recommend legal advice on notices, procedure and timing. From a surveying perspective I would advise on rental value, lease terms and negotiation strategy.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Commercial tenants always have the right to renew their lease.
challenge: What is security of tenure?
What does contracting out mean?
What is a Section 25 notice?
What is a Section 26 request?
keyPoints: The 1954 Act can give business tenants renewal rights
Contracting out changes the position
Landlords need statutory grounds to oppose renewal
Work with solicitors on legal process

Commercial Real Estate.q: What are the grounds for opposing lease renewal?
Commercial Real Estate.why: This question tests whether you understand that a landlord's ability to oppose renewal is limited where the tenant has statutory protection.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Where a tenant has security of tenure under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, the landlord can only oppose renewal on specific statutory grounds including tenant-related grounds such as failure to repair or persistent delay in paying rent, and landlord-related grounds such as intention to demolish or reconstruct the premises or occupy for own business purposes.
Commercial Real Estate.high: When advising a landlord I would first confirm whether the tenancy is protected and discuss whether any statutory ground may be available. It is important that the landlord has credible evidence to support the ground relied upon, particularly for redevelopment or own occupation. I would recommend legal advice to ensure notices and procedure are handled correctly — my role is to advise commercially while solicitors handle the legal process.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: The landlord can refuse to renew if they want the property back.
challenge: What is ground F?
Why is evidence important for redevelopment?
What happens if the landlord cannot prove the ground?
Are all grounds compensation-based?
keyPoints: A protected tenant cannot simply be removed at lease expiry
Opposition must be based on statutory grounds
Evidence is critical particularly for redevelopment
Surveyors advise commercially but legal process requires solicitors

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you advise a tenant approaching lease expiry?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to test whether you can provide practical client-focused advice to occupiers and understand the commercial and legal implications of lease expiry.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: When advising a tenant approaching lease expiry I would review the lease to confirm the expiry date, whether the lease is protected and whether there are any notice requirements. I would then discuss the tenant's business objectives — they may want to renew, relocate, downsize, expand or renegotiate terms.
Commercial Real Estate.high: If the tenant wants to remain I would advise on the likely renewal process, market rent and lease terms. If considering relocation I would assess alternative premises, timing, fit-out costs, business disruption and exit liabilities. I would also advise on dilapidations exposure and reinstatement obligations before lease expiry. My advice would be practical and time-sensitive because lease expiry decisions affect business continuity and negotiating strength.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would advise the tenant to negotiate a new lease as close to expiry as possible.
referralWhy: Fails to check security of tenure
Does not consider relocation or business continuity
challenge: Why is timing important before lease expiry?
What risks arise if the tenant leaves too late?
How would you advise on dilapidations?
What if the lease is contracted out?
keyPoints: Lease expiry advice should start early
Understand the lease and statutory position
Tenant objectives drive the strategy
Dilapidations timing and relocation costs can be as important as rent

Commercial Real Estate.q: What are the key risks associated with repairing obligations?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Repairing obligations are a major source of cost and dispute in commercial property. Assessors want to know whether candidates understand how lease wording can create significant liability.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Repairing obligations can create significant financial liability for tenants and income or asset protection issues for landlords. The first step is to review the lease wording carefully. For a tenant on a full repairing and insuring lease the obligation to keep the property in repair can be onerous if the property was already in poor condition.
Commercial Real Estate.high: For a tenant I would advise that repairing obligations should be considered before lease completion and recommend a schedule of condition to limit liability where appropriate. For a landlord I would consider whether the obligation protects asset value and whether it is enforceable. I would also advise that repairing obligations become particularly important at lease end where dilapidations claims can arise — specialist building surveying and legal input may be needed.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Repairing obligations just mean keeping the property tidy.
referralWhy: No mention of schedules of condition
challenge: What is an FRI lease?
How can a schedule of condition limit liability?
What are dilapidations?
Why should repair obligations be considered before lease completion?
keyPoints: Repairing obligations can create major financial exposure
Lease wording is critical
Tenants should understand liability before signing
Dilapidations risk should be considered early not only at lease expiry

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is Market Value?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors are not looking for a memorised definition. They want to see whether you understand how Market Value is applied and why the valuation basis matters.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Market Value is the estimated amount for which an asset or liability should exchange on the valuation date between a willing buyer and a willing seller, in an arm's-length transaction, after proper marketing, where both parties act knowledgeably, prudently and without compulsion.
Commercial Real Estate.high: In practice this means the valuation should reflect the market at the valuation date, assuming a proper marketing period and no special relationship between the parties. I would ensure the basis of value is clearly agreed within the terms of engagement and reported clearly to the client. The distinction between Market Value and price is important — price is the amount actually paid whereas value is a professional opinion based on evidence and assumptions at a specific date.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Market Value is what someone would pay for a property.
challenge: Why is the valuation date important?
What does arm's-length mean?
What is the difference between Market Value and Market Rent?
How does Market Value differ from investment value?
keyPoints: Market Value is a defined valuation basis
It reflects a hypothetical transaction at a specific date
It assumes willing knowledgeable parties
The valuation basis must be agreed and reported clearly

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is the Red Book?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to check that candidates understand when Red Book standards apply, why they matter and what terms of engagement are required.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: The Red Book is the RICS Valuation Global Standards. It sets out mandatory requirements and best practice guidance for valuation work undertaken by RICS members and regulated firms. Its purpose is to promote consistency, transparency and professional standards in valuation advice.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Before undertaking a valuation I would ensure terms of engagement are agreed with the client including the client, purpose of valuation, basis of value, valuation date, property interest, assumptions, limitations, fees and reporting requirements. I would also consider conflicts of interest and independence. If Red Book compliance is required the valuation must be prepared and reported in accordance with the relevant standards — if an exception or departure applies this must be properly justified and recorded.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: The Red Book is a valuation textbook.
referralWhy: Does not understand its mandatory nature
challenge: When does the Red Book apply?
What should be included in terms of engagement?
What is a conflict of interest in valuation?
Can a valuation ever be non-Red Book?
keyPoints: The Red Book governs professional valuation standards
It protects the client the public and the profession
Terms of engagement are essential
Independence competence and transparency are central

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you value a multi-let office building?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to see that you understand income, lease terms, risk and yield rather than simply applying a capital value per square foot.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: I would confirm the valuation purpose, basis of value and reporting requirements within the terms of engagement. I would inspect the property and review key information including floor areas, specification, condition, lease documents, tenancy schedule, service charge, rent review dates, lease expiries and any voids.
Commercial Real Estate.high: For an income-producing multi-let office I would use an investment method of valuation. I would assess the passing rent from each tenant, compare it with market rent and consider whether the property is rack-rented, reversionary or over-rented. I would assess income quality including lease length, break options and tenant covenant strength. I would then select an appropriate yield based on comparable investment transactions, adjusting for location, income security, lease profile, tenant quality and asset-specific risks.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would value it based on the total floor area and a rate per square foot.
referralWhy: Does not distinguish passing rent from market rent
challenge: What is a tenancy schedule?
What does reversionary mean?
How would you assess covenant strength?
How would void space affect value?
keyPoints: Multi-let offices are usually valued by analysing income
Lease terms and covenant strength affect risk
Passing rent and market rent must be compared
Yield selection must be evidence-based

Commercial Real Estate.q: What valuation approaches are commonly used in commercial property?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to avoid candidates who use valuation terminology without understanding when each method applies.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: The main valuation approaches include the comparable method, investment method, profits method, residual method and depreciated replacement cost. The comparable method is used where there is good transaction evidence. The investment method is used for income-producing property. The residual method is used for development sites.
Commercial Real Estate.high: The profits method may be used for trading properties such as hotels where value is linked to business performance. Depreciated replacement cost may be used where there is limited market evidence for specialised properties. The appropriate method depends on the property type, available evidence and purpose of valuation. Professional judgement is required when selecting and applying a method — it is not a formula.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would use the comparable method for most valuations.
referralWhy: Does not understand when each method applies
No understanding of residual or DRC
challenge: When would you use the investment method?
When might the residual method be appropriate?
Why might DRC be used?
Can more than one method be used?
keyPoints: Valuation method must match the property and purpose
Evidence quality is critical
Income-producing assets commonly valued by investment method
Professional judgement is required

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is investment value?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to see whether you understand that value can differ depending on the basis and the specific investor, and that candidates often confuse Market Value with investment value.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Investment value is the value of an asset to a particular owner or prospective owner for their individual investment or operational objectives. It differs from Market Value because Market Value reflects a hypothetical willing buyer and seller in the market, whereas investment value reflects the circumstances and requirements of a specific party.
Commercial Real Estate.high: For example a neighbouring owner may attribute a higher value to an adjoining property because it creates marriage value or unlocks a wider development opportunity — that value may not be reflected in Market Value. When advising a client I would be clear about the basis of value being used and explain that investment value is not necessarily the same as the price achievable in the open market.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Investment value is the value of an investment property.
referralWhy: Confuses investment value with Market Value
Does not understand special purchaser circumstances
Fails to explain basis of value
challenge: How does investment value differ from Market Value?
Can investment value be higher than Market Value?
What is marriage value?
How would you explain this to a client?
keyPoints: Investment value is specific to a particular investor
It may be higher or lower than Market Value
Client objectives can affect investment value
The valuation basis must be clearly stated

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is yield?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Yield is fundamental to commercial property valuation and investment. Assessors want to see whether you understand yield as a measure of return and risk, not just a calculation.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Yield is a measure of return from an investment property reflecting the relationship between income and capital value. At a simple level initial yield is calculated by dividing the current annual rent by the purchase price or capital value.
Commercial Real Estate.high: In practice different yields may be used depending on the income profile. Equivalent yield reflects the overall return from both current income and future reversionary income. Reversionary yield reflects the return once the property reaches market rent. Yield is also a measure of risk — a secure income stream from a strong tenant on a long lease may attract a lower yield resulting in a higher capital value. When advising a client I would support yield selection with comparable investment evidence and explain the risk factors that influence it.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Yield is the percentage return you get from a property.
referralWhy: Treats yield only as a formula
Does not link yield to risk
challenge: How do you calculate initial yield?
What is the relationship between yield and capital value?
Why might a risky asset have a higher yield?
What is reversionary yield?
keyPoints: Yield reflects return and risk
Yield and capital value move inversely
Secure income usually attracts lower yields
Yield selection must be evidence-based

Commercial Real Estate.q: How do yields affect capital values?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors ask this to test whether you understand the relationship between income, yield and value — candidates often understand terminology but struggle to explain the impact clearly.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: In commercial investment valuation capital value is strongly influenced by the relationship between income and yield. If income remains the same a lower yield produces a higher capital value because investors are willing to accept a lower return for an asset they see as lower risk. Conversely a higher yield produces a lower capital value.
Commercial Real Estate.high: A prime office let to a strong tenant on a long lease may attract a lower yield and therefore a higher capital value. A secondary asset with short income, vacancy risk or weak tenant covenant may attract a higher yield and lower value. When advising clients I would explain that changes in yield can significantly affect capital value even where the rent has not changed.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: A higher yield means a better investment.
referralWhy: Confuses rent increases with yield movement
challenge: What happens to value if yields move out?
What happens to value if yields harden?
How does tenant covenant affect yield?
How do interest rates affect investor demand?
keyPoints: Yield and capital value move inversely
Lower yield usually means higher capital value
Higher yield usually means lower capital value
Yield movement can materially affect investment performance

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you inspect a property for valuation purposes?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors want to see whether you understand that valuation inspection is purposeful, structured and linked to evidence, assumptions and risk.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Before inspecting I would review the terms of engagement to understand the purpose of the valuation, basis of value, property interest, inspection scope and any limitations. During the inspection I would consider location, access, surrounding uses, specification, accommodation, condition, configuration, services, occupancy and any visible defects.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would verify or record floor areas using the appropriate measurement basis, take inspection notes and photographs to support my valuation file, and identify matters requiring further investigation such as planning, title, environmental issues, contamination, building defects or EPC rating. Where I could not inspect parts of the property I would record the limitation and reflect this appropriately in my report or assumptions.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would walk around the property and take some photos.
referralWhy: Treats inspection as a casual walk-around
Does not link findings to value
challenge: What would you record during inspection?
How would you deal with inaccessible areas?
What measurement basis would you use?
What matters might require further investigation?
keyPoints: Valuation inspection supports the valuation opinion
Inspection scope should match the instruction
Limitations must be recorded
Physical legal market and environmental factors can all affect value

Commercial Real Estate.q: What are assumptions and special assumptions?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors ask this to check whether you understand how valuations rely on stated conditions and why these must be clear to the client as they can materially affect the valuation conclusion.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: An assumption is something accepted as true for the purpose of the valuation without requiring further investigation, provided it is reasonable. For example a valuer may assume good title, available services or no hidden defects unless evidence suggests otherwise. A special assumption assumes facts different from those existing at the valuation date or not normally made by market participants.
Commercial Real Estate.high: For example valuing a property on the assumption that planning consent has been granted when it has not yet been obtained would be a special assumption. Assumptions and special assumptions must be agreed with the client where appropriate and clearly stated in the valuation report because they can materially affect the valuation conclusion.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Assumptions are just standard things valuers always assume.
referralWhy: Fails to explain their impact on value
challenge: Give an example of an assumption
Give an example of a special assumption
Why must special assumptions be agreed?
What if an assumption later proves incorrect?
keyPoints: Assumptions are accepted facts for valuation purposes
Special assumptions depart from existing facts or normal market assumptions
Both must be clearly stated
Special assumptions can significantly affect value

Commercial Real Estate.q: What are the main risks within valuation instructions?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Valuation is a high-risk professional area. Assessors ask this to test whether you understand professional liability, client reliance and the importance of robust process.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Valuation instructions carry significant professional risk because clients and third parties may rely on the valuation for important financial decisions. The main risks include unclear instructions, using the wrong basis of value, conflicts of interest, lack of competence, insufficient evidence, inadequate inspection, incorrect assumptions and poor reporting.
Commercial Real Estate.high: To manage these risks I would ensure clear terms of engagement are agreed before starting the instruction confirming client, purpose, basis of value, valuation date, property interest, assumptions, limitations, fees and reporting requirements. I would consider whether I had appropriate competence and market knowledge, maintain a clear valuation file including inspection notes, evidence, calculations and reasoning. This supports the valuation conclusion and demonstrates a proper professional process. A valuation file should support the professional judgement reached.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: The main risk is getting the value wrong.
referralWhy: Does not mention terms of engagement
challenge: Why are terms of engagement important?
What would you do if you lacked local market knowledge?
How would you identify a conflict of interest?
What is client reliance?
keyPoints: Valuation risk is managed through process competence and evidence
Clear terms of engagement are essential
Conflicts and independence must be considered
A valuation file should support the professional judgement reached

Commercial Real Estate.q: What factors influence investment performance?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors test whether you understand commercial property as an investment asset and can explain how income, risk, market conditions and asset strategy influence performance.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Investment performance is influenced by both income return and capital growth. I would consider the strength and security of the income stream including tenant covenant, lease length, rent review pattern, break clauses and risk of voids. I would also consider potential for rental growth, asset management opportunities, capital expenditure requirements and wider market conditions.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Yield movement has a significant impact on capital value — if investor demand strengthens and yields move in, capital value may increase; if yields move out due to higher risk or weaker market sentiment, capital value may fall. Other important factors include location, specification, environmental performance, building condition, occupational demand, cost of finance and wider economic factors such as interest rates. A strong investment strategy should consider both current income and potential to improve future performance.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Investment performance is mainly about the rent you receive.
referralWhy: Forgets void risk and asset management
challenge: How does tenant covenant affect investment value?
What is the difference between income return and capital growth?
How do yield movements affect performance?
How can ESG influence investment performance?
keyPoints: Investment performance is driven by income risk and capital growth
Lease profile and tenant covenant are central to investment quality
Yield movement can materially affect value
Asset management can improve performance over time

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is a WAULT?
Commercial Real Estate.why: WAULT is a common investment metric. Assessors ask this to check whether you understand lease income duration and how it affects investment risk.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: WAULT stands for Weighted Average Unexpired Lease Term. It is a measure of the average remaining lease term across an investment property or portfolio, weighted by the rental income from each lease. It is used to assess income security.
Commercial Real Estate.high: A longer WAULT generally suggests more secure income assuming tenants are financially strong. A shorter WAULT may indicate higher lease event risk, potential vacancy or future reletting risk. WAULT can be calculated to lease expiry or to tenant break option — a property may appear to have five years to expiry but if there is a tenant break in two years the WAULT to break is materially shorter. When advising an investor I would consider WAULT alongside tenant covenant, rental levels, market demand and asset management opportunities.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: WAULT is just the average lease length across a property.
referralWhy: Does not understand it is weighted by income
Assumes longer WAULT is always positive
Does not link to investment risk
challenge: Why is WAULT weighted by income?
What is the difference between WAULT to expiry and WAULT to break?
Is a longer WAULT always better?
How would a short WAULT influence investor appetite?
keyPoints: WAULT measures income duration
It is weighted by rental income
Break options can materially change the risk profile
WAULT should be considered alongside covenant and market conditions

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you assess covenant strength?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Covenant strength affects income security, investment risk and valuation. Assessors want to know whether you can assess the reliability of a tenant's ability to meet lease obligations.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Covenant strength refers to the financial strength and reliability of a tenant and their ability to meet lease obligations. To assess it I would review the tenant's financial accounts, credit rating, payment history, business sector, trading performance and market reputation. I would also consider whether there is a parent company guarantee, rent deposit or other security.
Commercial Real Estate.high: For smaller or newer businesses I would assess risk more carefully and may advise the landlord to seek additional security such as a rent deposit or guarantor. Covenant strength affects investment value because secure income from a strong tenant is generally more attractive to investors and may support a lower yield. I would consider covenant alongside lease length, rent level, market demand and the ability to re-let if the tenant failed.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: A well-known brand is always a strong covenant.
referralWhy: Assumes brand recognition equals financial strength
Does not link covenant to value
challenge: What information would you request to assess covenant?
Why might a landlord require a rent deposit?
How does covenant strength affect yield?
Is a national tenant always a strong covenant?
keyPoints: Covenant strength affects income security
It should be assessed using evidence
Weak covenant may require additional security
Covenant strength influences investor appetite and yield

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is an asset management opportunity?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors test whether you can identify ways to improve asset performance and value and think commercially and proactively rather than just managing existing income.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: An asset management opportunity is an action that can improve the income, value, resilience or marketability of a property. Examples include letting vacant space, negotiating a lease regear, improving tenant covenant, carrying out refurbishment, improving energy performance, changing the tenant mix or repositioning the asset within the market.
Commercial Real Estate.high: When advising a client I would assess the cost, risk and likely return from each opportunity. Not every opportunity will be worthwhile — the advice must consider the client's objectives, capital availability, market demand and investment timescale. For example if an office building had a short WAULT and dated accommodation an asset management strategy might involve refurbishing vacant space, improving the EPC rating and negotiating longer lease commitments with existing tenants.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Asset management means maintaining the property and collecting rent.
referralWhy: Confuses asset management with property management
Lists opportunities without assessing cost or risk
challenge: How can refurbishment improve value?
What is a lease regear?
How might ESG create an asset management opportunity?
How would you assess whether an opportunity is viable?
keyPoints: Asset management is about improving performance
Opportunities must be commercially viable
Cost risk and return must be assessed
The best asset management advice aligns with the client's strategy

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you advise on a lease regear?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Lease regears are common commercial real estate transactions. Assessors want to see whether candidates understand the mutual benefit, negotiation points and impact on value.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: A lease regear involves renegotiating the terms of an existing lease, often before expiry, to create a revised agreement that benefits both landlord and tenant. For a landlord a regear may improve income security, extend the WAULT, remove a break option or support investment value. For a tenant it may secure more favourable terms such as a rent-free period, reduced rent or greater flexibility.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would first understand both parties' objectives and review the existing lease, current rent, lease expiry, break clauses, repair obligations and the tenant's covenant. I would assess the commercial impact of proposed changes — for example extending the lease term with a strong covenant tenant may improve investment value even if the landlord grants an incentive. My advice would compare the cost of any incentive or concession with the benefit of improved income security and reduced void risk.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: A regear just means giving the tenant what they want to keep them happy.
referralWhy: Thinks a regear only benefits tenants
Does not consider incentives and break clauses
challenge: Why might a landlord agree to a rent reduction?
How can a regear affect WAULT?
Why might a tenant request a regear?
How would you assess the value impact?
keyPoints: A lease regear changes existing lease terms
It should create commercial benefit for both parties
It can improve income security and investment value
The cost of concessions must be weighed against the benefit

Commercial Real Estate.q: What is a tenant retention strategy?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Tenant retention is central to protecting income and reducing void risk. Assessors test whether you understand occupier relationships and income security.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: A tenant retention strategy is an approach to keeping existing tenants in occupation where this supports the landlord's objectives. Retaining a good tenant protects income, reduces void periods, avoids reletting costs and may preserve investment value.
Commercial Real Estate.high: To advise on tenant retention I would monitor upcoming lease events such as break options, rent reviews and lease expiries and engage with the tenant to understand their business needs and future occupational requirements. If the tenant was important to the asset I may advise the landlord to consider a regear, refurbishment works or a commercially appropriate incentive. However retention is not always the best strategy — if the tenant is paying below market rent, has weak covenant or does not support the future positioning of the asset, reletting may be preferable.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: You should always try to keep your tenants.
referralWhy: Assumes all tenants should be retained
Ignores tenant covenant and market alternatives
Does not link retention to investment strategy
challenge: Why might tenant retention be valuable?
When might you not want to retain a tenant?
How do lease events affect retention strategy?
How does retention affect investment value?
keyPoints: Tenant retention protects income where the tenant supports the strategy
Existing tenants should be assessed commercially
Retention can reduce voids and reletting costs
Retention strategy should align with asset objectives

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you assess void risk?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Void risk affects income, value and investment performance. Assessors want to see whether you can identify and manage the risk of vacant space.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: To assess void risk I would review the lease profile to identify upcoming expiries, break options and rent reviews and assess the tenant's covenant strength and likelihood of remaining in occupation. I would then consider the property's marketability including location, specification, condition, rent level, EPC rating, amenities and competition from other available space.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would estimate the likely reletting period and costs including marketing, incentives, legal fees, refurbishment, empty rates and potential service charge shortfalls. If the risk was high I may advise early tenant engagement, lease regear discussions, targeted refurbishment or revised marketing strategy. Void risk should be considered in valuation and asset strategy because loss of income can materially affect performance.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: Void risk only becomes an issue when a tenant leaves.
referralWhy: Does not identify risk before vacancy occurs
Forgets empty rates and service charge shortfalls
challenge: Why do break options increase void risk?
What costs arise during a void period?
How can refurbishment reduce void risk?
How does void risk affect yield?
keyPoints: Void risk should be assessed before vacancy occurs
Lease events are key warning points
Void periods create direct and indirect costs
Asset management can reduce void risk

Commercial Real Estate.q: What due diligence would you undertake before acquisition?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Acquisition advice requires candidates to understand risk. Assessors want to see whether you can identify the information a client needs before committing to purchase.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Before acquisition I would undertake commercial due diligence to help the client understand the asset, income, risks and investment potential. I would review the tenancy schedule, leases, rent deposits, arrears, break options, rent reviews, lease expiries and tenant covenant strength. I would assess whether the income is secure, reversionary, over-rented or at risk.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would inspect the property and consider condition, specification, marketability, EPC rating, compliance issues and likely capital expenditure. Where needed I would recommend specialist building, environmental or legal advice. I would analyse market evidence to assess whether the purchase price is appropriate and consider future performance including rental growth, void risk and asset management opportunities. I would summarise key risks and opportunities so the client could make an informed decision before exchange.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would check the price is right and review the leases.
referralWhy: Fails to identify commercial risk and opportunity
challenge: Why is lease review important before acquisition?
How would you assess tenant covenant?
Why does EPC matter?
What specialist advice might be needed?
keyPoints: Acquisition due diligence protects the client from unknown risk
Income must be tested not assumed
Lease events condition and ESG can materially affect value
The surveyor's role is to identify commercial risk and opportunity

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would ESG influence investment advice?
Commercial Real Estate.why: ESG is now a significant factor in commercial real estate investment. Assessors want to see whether candidates understand how environmental, social and governance considerations affect risk, value and marketability.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: ESG can influence investment advice because it affects risk, occupier demand, operating costs, funding, marketability and long-term value. I would consider the property's EPC rating, energy efficiency, MEES compliance and likely future capital expenditure required to improve performance. Under current MEES regulations, most commercial properties cannot be let below EPC E. The government confirmed in 2026 a target of EPC B from 2031 for commercial buildings over 1,000 m² — a one-year extension from the earlier 2030 proposal, with the previously floated EPC C interim milestone for 2027 dropped entirely. Secondary legislation is still required, but this is confirmed government direction and should be informing acquisition strategy, hold period analysis and capital expenditure planning now.
Commercial Real Estate.high: A building with poor environmental performance may face reduced occupier demand, higher running costs, regulatory risk and potential value impact. For any commercial asset above 1,000 m², I would assess the gap between its current EPC rating and the EPC B target confirmed for 2031, model the improvement costs into acquisition advice, and consider how that capital expenditure affects pricing, returns and hold strategy. Existing flexibility mechanisms including the 7-year payback test and specific exemptions remain in place and should be reviewed where the EPC B requirement would otherwise be disproportionate. The dropped EPC C 2027 interim milestone is itself a material point — investors who were holding provisions against a 2027 compliance event need to understand that risk has been removed, replaced by the single 2031 EPC B target. Conversely a building with strong sustainability credentials may attract stronger occupier interest and investor demand. I would consider whether lease structures support ESG objectives through green lease provisions. When advising a client I would integrate ESG into asset strategy, acquisition due diligence, valuation risk and future capital expenditure planning — not treat it as a separate issue.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: ESG just means checking the EPC rating.
referralWhy: Treats ESG as only an EPC issue
Does not link ESG to value or risk
Gives generic sustainability comments without commercial relevance
challenge: What is MEES?
Why does EPC rating matter?
How can poor ESG performance affect value?
What is a green lease?
keyPoints: ESG affects value risk and marketability
EPC and MEES are important but not the whole picture
Poor ESG performance can create obsolescence risk
ESG should be built into investment and asset strategy

Commercial Real Estate.q: How would you advise on disposal strategy?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Disposal strategy tests whether candidates can advise on timing, pricing, market positioning and risk to help a client maximise value or achieve a strategic objective.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: When advising on disposal strategy I would begin by understanding the client's objectives — they may want to maximise price, sell quickly, reduce risk, recycle capital or dispose of a non-core asset. I would then assess the asset's current performance including income, lease profile, tenant covenant, WAULT, void risk, condition, EPC rating and capital expenditure requirements.
Commercial Real Estate.high: I would consider whether any pre-sale asset management could improve value such as settling a rent review, completing a letting, extending a lease or resolving title issues. I would advise on pricing strategy and method of sale — depending on the asset and market conditions this could involve private treaty, informal tender or a targeted off-market approach. I would identify likely purchaser groups and prepare clear marketing material and due diligence information. My advice would balance price, certainty, timing and execution risk.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would market the property and accept the highest offer.
referralWhy: Treats disposal as just marketing the property
Focuses only on price rather than certainty
challenge: Is the highest price always the best disposal outcome?
Why might pre-sale asset management be useful?
What is an informal tender?
How would market conditions influence timing?
keyPoints: Disposal strategy should reflect the client's objective
Timing and market conditions matter
Pre-sale preparation can improve value and certainty
The best offer is not always the highest offer if execution risk is high

Commercial Real Estate.q: Tell us about your APC case study.
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors open the discussion around your submission and test whether you genuinely understand the project you selected, your personal role, the client's objective, the key issue, the advice you gave and the outcome.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: My case study concerned a commercial property instruction where my client required advice on a key issue. My role was to review relevant property information, analyse market evidence, identify the main risks and prepare advice for the client. The client's objective was clearly defined and I considered available options before making my recommendation.
Commercial Real Estate.high: The strongest case study answers are structured and concise — assessors want your role not the whole project story. I would explain the client's objective, the key challenge and why it mattered commercially, the options I considered, my recommendation and why it was appropriate, the outcome and my main learning point. Using I rather than we throughout is essential to demonstrate personal involvement.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: The project involved a large team and we successfully completed the transaction.
challenge: What was your personal role?
Why did you choose this case study?
What was the key professional judgement?
What would you do differently?
keyPoints: Assessors want your role not the whole project story
Structure answers concisely
Explain advice and reasoning not just events
Reflection demonstrates professional maturity

Commercial Real Estate.q: Why was your advice appropriate?
Commercial Real Estate.why: This is one of the most important final assessment questions because it tests professional judgement. Assessors want to know whether your recommendation was reasoned, proportionate and in the client's best interests.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: My advice was appropriate because it was based on the client's stated objective, the evidence available and the risks identified during the instruction. I did not simply recommend the most attractive option on the surface — I considered the alternatives and assessed each against the client's priorities.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Although one option may have produced a stronger headline position, it carried greater execution risk. My recommendation balanced the potential benefit with the likelihood of achieving the desired outcome. I communicated the limitations of my advice and recommended specialist input where appropriate, ensuring the client understood the basis of my recommendation and could make an informed decision.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: My advice was appropriate because the client accepted it.
referralWhy: No explanation of evidence or reasoning
challenge: What evidence supported your advice?
What risks did you identify?
What alternatives were rejected and why?
Would your advice change with hindsight?
keyPoints: Appropriate advice is evidence-based and client-specific
Assessors want the reasoning behind the recommendation
Strong candidates explain why alternatives were not chosen
Link advice to risk outcome and client objective

Commercial Real Estate.q: What alternatives did you consider?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors test whether you exercised judgement rather than simply following one route. Commercial Real Estate candidates should explain the options available and why the selected course of action was preferred.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: I considered several alternatives before making my recommendation. I assessed the advantages and disadvantages of each option against the client's objective, considering cost, timing, risk, deliverability and commercial impact.
Commercial Real Estate.high: The first option had certain advantages but carried risk in relation to cost or timing. The second option may have achieved a different benefit but carried execution uncertainty. The third option was most aligned with the client's objective because it provided the best balance between commercial benefit, deliverability and risk. I made sure the client understood why the other options were not preferred.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: There was really only one option that made sense.
referralWhy: Demonstrates no judgement or alternatives considered
Not linking decision to client objective
challenge: Which option carried the greatest risk?
Did the client disagree with your recommendation?
What would have happened if the client chose another option?
How did you communicate the alternatives?
keyPoints: Level 3 advice usually involves evaluating options
Assessors want to see judgement not hindsight
Alternatives should be realistic
Strong answers explain why an option was rejected

Commercial Real Estate.q: What was the greatest commercial risk?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors test whether you understood the commercial consequences of your advice and can identify risk, explain its impact and advise on mitigation.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: The greatest commercial risk was one that had the potential to affect income, value, occupation, timing, cost, transaction certainty or client liability. I assessed the risk by reviewing market evidence, lease terms, tenant covenant, comparable transactions, building condition or legal information.
Commercial Real Estate.high: To mitigate the risk I advised on specific actions which allowed the client to make a more informed decision. I also explained any residual risk that could not be fully removed. For example in a letting instruction the greatest risk may have been an extended void period if the property was marketed at an unrealistic rent — I would advise on rental strategy and review market feedback regularly.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: The greatest risk was that the deal might not complete.
referralWhy: Chooses a minor or vague risk
Describes the problem but not the impact
challenge: How did you identify the risk?
What would have happened if the risk was ignored?
How did you communicate the risk to the client?
Was the risk fully mitigated?
keyPoints: Commercial risk must be linked to client impact
Strong candidates explain both risk and mitigation
Not all risk can be eliminated
Assessors want commercial awareness not just technical knowledge

Commercial Real Estate.q: How did you protect your client's interests?
Commercial Real Estate.why: This question tests client care, professional judgement and ethical awareness. Assessors want to see whether you acted in the client's best interests while remaining professional, objective and within your competence.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: I protected my client's interests by first making sure I understood their objective and the commercial outcome they wanted to achieve. I reviewed the relevant evidence, identified the main risks that could affect the client's position and explained those risks clearly including their potential financial and operational impact.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Where the client's preferred approach carried risk I advised them on the implications rather than simply agreeing with their view. I documented my advice and recommended specialist legal or technical input where issues fell outside my competence. My aim was to support the client's objective while ensuring they made an informed decision — protecting the client is not the same as simply obeying the client.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I did whatever the client asked me to do.
challenge: Did your client ever disagree with your advice?
How did you manage expectations?
How did you record your advice?
How did you balance commercial pressure with professional standards?
keyPoints: Protecting the client is not the same as simply obeying the client
Clients need clear reasoned and honest advice
Advice should be documented
Professional judgement includes knowing when to recommend specialist input

Commercial Real Estate.q: How did you negotiate a successful outcome?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Negotiation is central to Commercial Real Estate practice. Assessors test whether you can prepare, communicate and reach an outcome that supports the client's objective.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: I began by agreeing the client's objectives and understanding the acceptable negotiation range. I then prepared my position using relevant evidence including comparable transactions, market conditions and the specific facts of the instruction. I also considered the likely priorities of the other party to identify where there may be room for compromise.
Commercial Real Estate.high: During the negotiation I presented my position clearly and supported it with evidence. I listened to the other party's points and tested whether their position was evidence-based. Where appropriate I advised the client on the benefits of settlement rather than pursuing a more aggressive position that could create delay or risk. The outcome was successful because it achieved the client's commercial objective while remaining proportionate.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I negotiated hard until I got the best deal.
referralWhy: Does not explain preparation or evidence
Does not link outcome to client objective
challenge: What was your opening position?
What was your fall-back position?
How did you use evidence in negotiation?
How did you know the outcome was successful?
keyPoints: Good negotiation is prepared evidence-based and professional
A successful outcome is not always the most aggressive outcome
Understanding the other party can improve results
Settlement should be assessed against client objectives and risk

Commercial Real Estate.q: How did sustainability influence your recommendation?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Sustainability is increasingly relevant across Commercial Real Estate. Assessors want to see whether candidates can link sustainability to commercial advice not just make general ESG statements.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: Sustainability influenced my recommendation because it affected the property's marketability, future risk and potential value. I considered the EPC rating, likely MEES compliance position, energy performance, occupier expectations and any capital expenditure required to improve the building.
Commercial Real Estate.high: Where a property had a weaker EPC rating I advised the client that this could affect future letting prospects, investor demand and compliance risk. I recommended that sustainability improvements should be considered as part of the wider asset strategy rather than treated as a separate issue. My recommendation balanced commercial return with future resilience and I explained that sustainability can influence both occupational demand and long-term investment performance.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I mentioned the EPC rating in my report.
referralWhy: Does not link sustainability to value or marketability
challenge: What is MEES?
How can EPC rating affect value?
How does ESG influence occupier demand?
Did sustainability change your final recommendation?
keyPoints: Sustainability must be linked to commercial decision-making
EPC and MEES can affect lettability and value
ESG expectations are increasingly important to occupiers and investors
Strong candidates explain sustainability as part of risk and strategy

Commercial Real Estate.q: What would you do differently?
Commercial Real Estate.why: Assessors test reflection, professional maturity and learning. They are not looking for a perfect candidate — they are looking for someone who can evaluate their own performance and improve.
Commercial Real Estate.pass: With hindsight I would have taken a specific action that would have helped achieve a better outcome — for example engaging with the client earlier on a particular risk, gathering additional comparable evidence at an earlier stage or documenting an assumption more clearly.
Commercial Real Estate.high: The key learning for me was a specific insight that I have since applied to improve the way I approach similar instructions. I would not change my overall recommendation if I still believed it was supported by the evidence, but I would improve the process in a specific way. Assessors expect learning not perfection — the answer should be specific and credible.
Commercial Real Estate.referral: I would not do anything differently — the advice was correct.
referralWhy: Does not explain how learning was applied
Suggesting the whole advice was wrong without explanation
challenge: Did anything go wrong?
What did you learn?
How have you applied that learning since?
How did you seek feedback?
keyPoints: Reflection is a strength when handled well
Assessors expect learning not perfection
The answer should be specific and credible
